Aspects of the commuting graph Note: To the memory of Richard Parker

Abstract

Our purpose in this paper is twofold.

  1. (a)

    We discuss the computational problem of deciding whether a given graph is the commuting graph of a finite group; we give a quasipolynomial algorithm, and a polynomial algorithm for the case when the group is an extraspecial pp-group for pp an odd prime.

  2. (b)

    We give new results on the question of whether the commuting graph of a given group is a cograph or a chordal graph, two classes of graphs defined by forbidden subgraphs.

The problems are not unrelated, since there are a number of cases where hard computational problems on graphs are easier when restricted to special classes of graphs; we conjecture that the recognition problem is polynomial for cographs and chordal graphs.

Keywords: 
finite group , commuting graph , forbidden subgraph , cograph , chordal graph , graph isomorphism , quasipolynomial algorithm , extraspecial group

1 Introduction

Graphs associated with some algebraic structures, such as the power graph of a group or semigroup, have been actively investigated (cf. [1, 21, 23, 25]) Of course the famous Cayley graphs have a long history. Moreover, graphs from algebraic structures have valuable applications (cf. [48]): for example, Cayley graphs as classifiers for data mining [49].

Let GG be a group and SS be a subset of GG. The commuting graph of GG on SS is a simple graph with vertex set SS, and two distinct elements are adjacent in this graph if they commute in GG. In particular, if S=GS=G, then we denote this commuting graph on GG by Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). In 1955, Brauer and Fowler [12] first introduced the commuting graph of a group and showed that there are only finitely many simple groups with even order such that they have a prescribed involution centralizer. In fact, in the seminal paper [12], they considered the induced subgraph of the commuting graph on the set of all non-trivial elements of the group. Since then, the commuting graphs have received considerable attention and have been well studied in the literature. For example, Segev et al. [69, 70, 71] established some longstanding conjectures on division algebras by using combinatorial parameters of commuting graphs. Britnell and Gill [15] classified all finite quasi-simple groups GG whose commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is perfect, where Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is defined on the vertex set G∖Z⁡(G)G\setminus Z(G), where Z⁡(G)Z(G) is the centre of GG. Giudici and Parker [40] showed that for every positive integer dd, there is a finite 22-group GG such that the commuting graph of GG on the set of all non-central elements has diameter greater than dd; further results are found in [31]. Morgan and Parker [62] proved that, for a finite group GG with trivial centre, every connected component of the commuting graph of GG on the set of all non-trivial elements has diameter at most 1010. Recently, Beike et al. [9] extended some of their results; some further applications of commuting graphs in group theory can be found in [22].

The first part of this paper is devoted to the following algorithmic question.

Question 1

Given a simple undirected graph Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E), with vertex set VV and edge set EE, is it isomorphic to the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) of a group GG? More precisely, is there a bijection φ:V→G\varphi:V\to G such that a vertex pair {u,v}\{u,v\} is an edge in Γ\Gamma precisely when the groups elements φ⁡(u),φ⁡(v)∈G\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\in G commute.

We give a quasi-polynomial algorithm to answer this question in general, and a polynomial-time algorithm in the case of extraspecial pp-groups with pp odd.

A number of important graph classes, including perfect graphs, cographs, chordal graphs, split graphs, and threshold graphs, can be defined either structurally or in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs. Forbidden subgraphs of power graphs were studied in [58]. In [22], the second author proposed the following question.

Question 2

([22, Question 14]) For which finite groups is the commuting graph a perfect graph, or a cograph, or a chordal graph, or a split graph, or a threshold graph?

Britnell and Gill [15] studied the finite groups whose commuting graph is perfect. The second and third authors [54] completely classified the finite groups whose commuting graph is a split graph or a threshold graph.

In Part II of the paper (Sections 10, 11, 12, and 13) , we address the question of when the commuting graph is a cograph or a chordal graph. We prove that in some sense, the class of such groups generalizes the class of finite solvable groups (see Theorem 11.7 in Subsection 11.3). Also we determine all finite simple groups whose commuting graph is a cograph (see Problem 1 in Subsection 11.3 and Theorem 12.16 at the end of Section 12). The results partly answer Question 2.

These questions are relevant to the recognition problem (Question 1). There are extra hypotheses which could make the problem of recognition of commuting graphs easier and yield faster algorithms. One is to restrict the groups to a known class, such as nilpotent groups. Another is to restrict the graphs to a class in which computation is easier. For example, the result of the second and third authors [54] describes precisely the split or threshold graphs which are commuting graphs; these are the complete graphs, together with the graphs consisting of an nn-vertex complete graph (where nn is odd), with nn pendant edges added at one of its vertices. Clearly these are easily recognised.

We note that some works, especially on connectedness and diameter, define the commuting graph to have vertex set G∖Z⁡(G)G\setminus Z(G) (that is, omitting dominating vertices). This has little effect on our results. For the recognition problem, if we are given the commuting graph on G∖Z⁡(G)G\setminus Z(G), then the commuting graph on GG is found by adding |Z⁡(G)||Z(G)| dominating vertices to the graph, and this number is a divisor of |G∖Z⁡(G)||G\setminus Z(G)| so there are not many possibilities. In the second part of the paper too, as mentioned before Proposition 10.2, we can define the commuting graph without including the centre Z⁡(G)Z(G) and the results essentially remain the same.

We conclude the introduction with a suggestion for further research, which would link the two parts of the paper together more closely.

Question 3

Suppose that Γ\Gamma is a perfect graph, a cograph or a chordal graph. Is there a polynomial algorithm to decide whether Γ\Gamma is the commuting graph of a group?

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we will introduce some notation and recall some definitions on groups and graphs.

Every group considered is finite. Throughout, GG always denotes a finite group and 1G1_{G} denotes the identity element of GG, and we denote 1G1_{G} simply by 11 if the considered group is unambiguous. The order of the group GG is its cardinality, denoted |G||G|. For an element g∈Gg\in G, the order o⁡(g)o(g) of gg in GG is the size of the cyclic subgroup ⟨g⟩\langle g\rangle generated by gg. The element gg is called an involution if o⁡(g)=2o(g)=2. The centre of GG, denoted by Z⁡(G)Z(G), is defined as the subgroup

{x∈G:g​x=x​g​ for each g∈G}.\{x\in G:gx=xg\hbox{ for each $g\in G$}\}.

The centralizer CG​(g)C_{G}(g) of gg in GG is the subgroup of all elements that commute with gg, that is,

CG​(g)={x∈G:g​x=x​g}.C_{G}(g)=\{x\in G:gx=xg\}.

The commutator of two elements x,yx,y is denoted as [x,y][x,y], that is, [x,y]=x−1​y−1​x​y[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy. Note that xx and yy commute if and only if [x,y]=1[x,y]=1. The derived group, or commutator subgroup, G′G^{\prime} of GG is the subgroup generated by all commutators. The derived series is the series of subgroups G(n)G^{(n)} of GG defined by G0=GG^{0}=G and G(n+1)=(G(n))′G^{(n+1)}=(G^{(n)})^{\prime}. The group GG is solvable if G(n)=1G^{(n)}=1 for some nn.

Denote by ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} the cyclic group with order nn. For a prime pp, a pp-group is a group whose order is a power of pp. An elementary abelian pp-group is a pp-group that is a direct product of cyclic groups of order pp. A Sylow pp-subgroup of GG is a pp-subgroup whose index in GG is coprime to pp.

An automorphism of GG is a permutation α\alpha of GG preserving the group operation: (g​h)α=gα​hα(gh)^{\alpha}=g^{\alpha}h^{\alpha}. An inner automorphism is a map ϕ⁡(g):x↦g−1​x​g\phi(g):x\mapsto g^{-1}xg. It is readily checked that the automorphisms of GG form a group Aut(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G), while the inner automorphisms form a subgroup Inn(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G) of Aut(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G).

A subgroup NN of GG is a normal subgroup of GG, denoted N⊲GN\lhd G, if g​N=N​ggN=Ng for all g∈Gg\in G. The quotient G/NG/N is the group whose elements are the cosets of NN in GG with the (well-defined) group operation (N​g1)​(N​g2)=N⁡(g1​g2)(Ng_{1})(Ng_{2})=N(g_{1}g_{2}). For example,

  • (a)

    the centre Z⁡(G)Z(G) is a normal subgroup of GG, and G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G) is isomorphic to Inn(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G);

  • (b)

    the inner automorphism group Inn(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G) is a normal subgroup of the automorphism group Aut(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G); the quotient is the outer automorphism group Out(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Out}}(G) of GG;

  • (c)

    the derived group G′G^{\prime} is a normal subgroup of GG; it is the smallest normal subgroup NN for which G/NG/N is abelian.

A subgroup of GG is characteristic if it is mapped to itself by all automorphisms of GG. Since a subgroup is normal if it is mapped to itself by all inner automorphisms, we see that each characteristic subgroup is normal.

A group GG is simple if its only normal subgroups are GG and {1}\{1\}. In this paper, we will use the Classification of the Finite Simple Groups (CFSG), which will be explained when it is used in Section 8.1. Here we note one consequence of CFSG, the proof of the Schreier conjecture:

Theorem 2.1

If GG is a non-abelian finite simple group, then Out(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Out}}(G) is solvable.

Each minimal (non-trivial) normal subgroup of a finite group is a direct product of isomorphic simple groups [33, Theorem 4.3A(iii)]. The socle of GG, denoted Soc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Soc}}(G), is the product of the minimal normal subgroups of GG; it is a direct product of simple groups (not necessarily isomorphic). If the socle is simple, we say that GG is almost simple.

A normal series for a group GG is a collection of normal subgroups Ni⊲GN_{i}\lhd G with 0≤i≤r0\leq i\leq r such that

{1}=N0⊂N1⊂N2⊂⋯⊂Nr=G.\{1\}=N_{0}\subset N_{1}\subset N_{2}\subset\cdots\subset N_{r}=G.

This series is a central series for GG if Ni/Ni−1⊆Z⁡(G/Ni−1)N_{i}/N_{i-1}\subseteq Z(G/N_{i-1}) for 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r. A group GG is nilpotent if it has a central series. If GG is nilpotent, and we build the upper central series by taking Ni/Ni−1=Z⁡(G/Ni−1)N_{i}/N_{i-1}=Z(G/N_{i-1}), the number of steps in the series is the nilpotency class of GG.

Theorem 2.2

[46, Theorem 1.26] If GG is a finite group, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    GG is nilpotent.

  2. (b)

    Every Sylow subgroup of GG is normal in GG.

  3. (c)

    GG is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups.

A central product H∘KH\circ K of two groups HH and KK with respect to an isomorphism θ\theta from a central subgroup ZZ of HH to a central subgroup of KK is defined to be

(H×K)/{(z,z​θ):z∈Z}.(H\times K)/\{(z,z\theta):z\in Z\}.

By F⁡(G)F(G) we will denote the Fitting subgroup of GG, i.e. the largest normal nilpotent subgroup of GG.

A component of GG is a subgroup HH of GG which is quasisimple (that is, H=H′H=H^{\prime} and H/Z⁡(H)H/Z(H) is simple) and subnormal in GG (that is, a term in some normal series of GG). Let Comp(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G) be the set of components of GG. Then the subgroup E⁡(G)E(G) is the subgroup generated by Comp(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G), and the generalized Fitting subgroup F∗​(G)F^{*}(G) of GG is the central product

F∗​(G)=F⁡(G)∘E⁡(G),F^{*}(G)=F(G)\circ E(G), (1)

see [3, 31.12].

Given a positive integer nn, we use D2​nD_{2n} to denote the dihedral group with order 2​n2n. A presentation of D2​nD_{2n} is given by

D2​n=⟨a,b:an=b2=1,bab=a−1⟩.D_{2n}=\langle a,b:a^{n}=b^{2}=1,bab=a^{-1}\rangle. (2)

Note that D2​nD_{2n} is an abelian group if and only if n∈{1,2}n\in\{1,2\}, and for all 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

o⁡(ai​b)=2,D2​n=⟨a⟩∪{b,a​b,a2​b,…,an−1​b}.o(a^{i}b)=2,~~D_{2n}=\langle a\rangle\cup\{b,ab,a^{2}b,\ldots,a^{n-1}b\}. (3)

Suppose that AA is an abelian group. The generalized dihedral group corresponding to AA, denoted by D⁡(A)D(A), is the external semidirect product A⋊TA\rtimes T of AA with the cyclic group T=⟨t⟩T=\langle t\rangle of order two, with the non-identity element tt acting as the inverse map on AA, that is,

xt=x−1​ for all ​x∈A.x^{t}=x^{-1}\textrm{ for all }x\in A.

Viewing this as an internal semidirect product, AA is an abelian normal subgroup of D⁡(A)D(A) of index two. A presentation for D⁡(A)D(A) is as follows:

D(A)=⟨A,t:o(t)=2,tgt=g−1 for each g∈A⟩.D(A)=\langle A,t:o(t)=2,tgt=g^{-1}\hbox{ for each $g\in A$}\rangle. (4)
Observation 1

Let D⁡(A)D(A) be the generalized dihedral group as presented in (4). Then we have the following.

  • (i)

    Every element of D⁡(A)∖AD(A)\setminus A is an involution;

  • (ii)

    D⁡(A)D(A) is abelian if and only if AA is an elementary abelian 22-group, if and only if D⁡(A)D(A) is an elementary abelian 22-group;

  • (iii)

    If AA is cyclic of order nn, then D⁡(A)≅D⁡(ℤn)≅D2​nD(A)\cong D(\mathbb{Z}_{n})\cong D_{2n}.

Proof 1

As AA is a normal subgroup of D⁡(A)D(A) of index two, every element g∈D⁡(A)∖Ag\in D(A)\setminus A is in the coset A​tAt and is of the form g=a​tg=at. Hence, g2=a​t​a​t=a​at=a​a−1=1g^{2}=atat=aa^{t}=aa^{-1}=1 which means gg is an involution. Furthermore, D⁡(A)D(A) is commutative if and only if for all a∈Aa\in A, a​t=t​aat=ta. That is, t​a​t=a−1=atat=a^{-1}=a which implies a2=1a^{2}=1 for all a∈Aa\in A, implying that AA is an elementary abelian 22-group which, in turn, implies that D⁡(A)D(A) is an elementary abelian 22-group. The last part follows directly from the definition of dihedral groups. ∎

Observation 1(ii) means that D⁡(A)D(A) is non-abelian if and only if AA has an element of order at least 33. Moreover, Observation 1(iii) implies that the dihedral groups are special cases of generalized dihedral groups. As an example, one can check that D⁡(ℤ2×ℤ6)≅ℤ2×D12D(\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{6})\cong\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times D_{12}.

Given a positive integer mm at least 22, Johnson [47, pp. 44–45] introduced the generalized quaternion group Q4​mQ_{4m} of order 4​m4m, that is,

Q4​m=⟨x,y:xm=y2,x2​m=1,y−1xy=x−1⟩.Q_{4m}=\langle x,y:x^{m}=y^{2},x^{2m}=1,y^{-1}xy=x^{-1}\rangle. (5)
Observation 2

For any 1≤i≤2​m1\leq i\leq 2m, o⁡(xi​y)=4o(x^{i}y)=4 and Z⁡(Q4​m)={1,xm}Z(Q_{4m})=\{1,x^{m}\}.

Proof 2

By definition, x2​m=y4=1x^{2m}=y^{4}=1, which implies that o⁡(y)=4o(y)=4, as there are no other relations. Furthermore, as x​y=y​x−1xy=yx^{-1} we can write xi​y=y​x−ix^{i}y=yx^{-i} for any positive integer ii. It follows that xi​y​xi​y=y​x−i​xi​y=y2x^{i}yx^{i}y=yx^{-i}x^{i}y=y^{2} for all ii. Hence, (xi​y)4=y4=1(x^{i}y)^{4}=y^{4}=1 for all ii, implying that o⁡(xi​y)=4o(x^{i}y)=4 for 1≤i≤2​m1\leq i\leq 2m. We can express every element in Q4​mQ_{4m} as xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} for 0≤i≤2​m−10\leq i\leq 2m-1 and 0≤j≤30\leq j\leq 3. Now, the element xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} is in the centre Z⁡(Q4​m)Z(Q_{4m}) if and only if it commutes with both yy and xx. Clearly, y​xi​yj=xi​yj​yyx^{i}y^{j}=x^{i}y^{j}y if and only if y​xi=xi​yyx^{i}=x^{i}y if and only if y​xi=y​x−iyx^{i}=yx^{-i}, which is equivalent to x2​i=1x^{2i}=1. This forces i∈{0,m}i\in\{0,m\}. Thus, xmx^{m} is in the centre Z⁡(Q4​m)Z(Q_{4m}). Suppose j∈{0,2}j\in\{0,2\}. If j∈{0,2}j\in\{0,2\} then, as i∈{0,m}i\in\{0,m\}, and xm=y2x^{m}=y^{2} by definition of the group Q4​mQ_{4m}, it follows that xi​yj∈{1,xm}x^{i}y^{j}\in\{1,x^{m}\} which is contained in the centre Z⁡(Q4​m)Z(Q_{4m}). Consider the case j∈{1,3}j\in\{1,3\}. Then xm​yj​x=xm+1​yjx^{m}y^{j}x=x^{m+1}y^{j} if and only if yj​x=x​yjy^{j}x=xy^{j}, which is equivalent to yj​x=yj​x−1y^{j}x=y^{j}x^{-1} as x​yj=yj​x−1xy^{j}=y^{j}x^{-1} since jj is odd. But that implies x2=1x^{2}=1 which is a contradiction as o⁡(x)=2​m>2o(x)=2m>2. Hence Z⁡(Q4​m)={1,xm}Z(Q_{4m})=\{1,x^{m}\}. ∎

The group of all permutations of {1,2,…,n}\{1,2,\ldots,n\} is the symmetric group SnS_{n}. For n≥2n\geq 2, its derived group is the alternating group AnA_{n} consisting of all even permutations. The alternating group is simple for n≥5n\geq 5.

A group GG is called a Frobenius group if there is a proper subgroup HH of GG such that H∩Hg=1H\cap H^{g}=1 whenever g∈G∖Hg\in G\setminus H. Let

K={1G}∪(G∖(∪g∈GHg))K=\{1_{G}\}\cup(G\setminus(\cup_{g\in G}H^{g}))

be the Frobenius kernel of GG. It is well-known (see, for example, [3, 35.24 and 35.25]) that K​⊴​GK\trianglelefteq G, G=K⋊HG=K\rtimes H, CG​(h)≤HC_{G}(h)\leq H for each h∈Hh\in H, and CG​(k)≤KC_{G}(k)\leq K for each k∈K∖{1}k\in K\setminus\{1\}. Moreover, by the Thompson theorem on finite groups with fixed-point-free automorphisms of prime order [79, Theorem 1], KK is nilpotent. Frobenius groups are also characterised as transitive non-regular permutation groups in which non-identity elements fix at most one point.

The Frattini subgroup Φ⁡(G)\Phi(G) of a finite group GG is the intersection of all maximal proper subgroups of GG. A pp-group GG is an extraspecial group GG if its centre Z⁡(G)Z(G) is of order pp and coincides with its derived subgroup G′G^{\prime} and the Frattini subgroup Φ⁡(G)\Phi(G) [46, Chapter 4, pp. 123]. Furthermore, there are exactly two non-isomorphic extraspecial groups of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, for each r≥1r\geq 1 and each prime pp.

Every graph considered in this paper is simple: that is, it is undirected, with no loops and no multiple edges. Given a graph Γ\Gamma, the vertex set and edge set of Γ\Gamma are denoted by V⁡(Γ)V(\Gamma) and E⁡(Γ)E(\Gamma), respectively. We often write Γ\Gamma as a pair Γ=(V,E)\Gamma=(V,E) where V=V⁡(Γ)V=V(\Gamma) and E=E⁡(Γ)E=E(\Gamma). For a vertex subset U⊂V⁡(Γ)U\subset V(\Gamma) the induced subgraph Γ⁡[U]\Gamma[U] has vertex set UU and edge set {{u,v}∈E(Γ)∣u,v∈U}\{\{u,v\}\in E(\Gamma)\mid u,v\in U\}. In other words, the subgraph induced by UU has vertex set UU and its edge set consists of all edges of Γ\Gamma between vertices in UU.

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a collection of finite graphs. If no induced subgraph of Γ\Gamma is isomorphic to a graph in ℱ\mathcal{F}, then Γ\Gamma is called ℱ\mathcal{F}-free; and if ℱ={Δ}\mathcal{F}=\{\Delta\}, for some graph Δ\Delta, we say that Γ\Gamma is Δ\Delta-free. Sometimes we say instead that Γ\Gamma forbids ℱ\mathcal{F} or Δ\Delta. Denote by PnP_{n} and CnC_{n} the path of length n−1n-1 and the cycle of length nn, respectively. For distinct x,y∈V⁡(Γ)x,y\in V(\Gamma), if xx is adjacent to yy in Γ\Gamma, then we write x∼Γyx\sim_{\Gamma}y to denote this edge {x,y}\{x,y\}, or just by x∼yx\sim y when Γ\Gamma is clear from the context. In particular, if PnP_{n} is the subgraph of Γ\Gamma induced by the vertex subset {x1,x2,…,xn}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\} with the only adjacencies being xi∼xi+1x_{i}\sim x_{i+1}, for each 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, we denote the induced path PnP_{n} by

x1∼x2∼⋯∼xn.x_{1}\sim x_{2}\sim\cdots\sim x_{n}.

Similarly, in Γ\Gamma, if the nn-cycle CnC_{n} is the subgraph induced by the subset of vertices {x1,x2,…,xn}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}\}, where the only edges between them are {x1,xn}∈E⁡(Γ)\{x_{1},x_{n}\}\in E(\Gamma) and {xi,xi+1}∈E⁡(Γ)\{x_{i},x_{i+1}\}\in E(\Gamma) for all 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, we denote it by

x1∼x2∼⋯∼xn∼x1.x_{1}\sim x_{2}\sim\cdots\sim x_{n}\sim x_{1}.

The neighbourhood of a vertex vv is N⁡(v)={w∈V⁡(Γ):w∼v}N(v)=\{w\in V(\Gamma):w\sim v\}, and the closed neighbourhood of vv is N¯​(v)={v}∪N​(v)\bar{N}(v)=\{v\}\cup N(v). A vertex vv of a graph Γ\Gamma is said to be dominating if v∼wv\sim w for all w∈V⁡(Γ)∖{v}w\in V(\Gamma)\setminus\{v\}.

Part I Recognising the commuting graph

3 The Recognition Problem

The main focus of this part is the recognition problem of commuting graphs. It is basically an algorithmic question. Given an undirected graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) as input, the aim is to design an algorithm that efficiently checks if there is a group GG with |V||V| elements such that the input graph XX is isomorphic to Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), and if so to efficiently determine such an isomorphism.

We summarize our results.

  • (a)

    We obtain a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the case of extraspecial pp-groups for odd primes pp. Extraspecial pp-groups are a special case of pp-groups of nilpotence class 22. A formal definition is in Section 7.

  • (b)

    For the general case, we obtain a quasipolynomial-time algorithm for the recognition problem of commuting graphs. The algorithm is essentially based on a simple 2O⁡(log3⁡n)2^{O(\log^{3}n)} time algorithm that enumerates the multiplication tables of all distinct groups of order nn (where by distinct we mean mutually non-isomorphic groups of order nn). This enumeration algorithm combined with Babai’s quasipolynomial time algorithm for graph isomorphism [4] yields a simple 2O⁡(log3⁡n)2^{O(\log^{3}n)} time algorithm to check if a given nn-vertex graph XX is the commuting graph of a group of order nn: for each nn-element group GG that is output by the enumeration algorithm we check if Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is isomorphic to XX by using Babai’s isomorphism test [4].

  • (c)

    A natural question in connection with our algorithm for recognizing the commuting graphs of extraspecial groups is whether groups with the same commuting graphs are isoclinic. This holds for extraspecial groups (this is exploited by the algorithm), and it is natural to conjecture that this property holds for all groups of nilpotence class 2 (of which extraspecial groups are a subclass). We present counter-examples for class-3 nilpotent groups and conjecture that the property holds for class-2 nilpotent groups.

  • (d)

    Additionally, we also show an efficient reduction of the commuting graph recognition problem to the recognition problem of commuting graphs of indecomposable groups. We also note recognizing the commuting graph of generalized dihedral groups along with an extension to Frobenius groups.

Some related work.  There is a result by Giudici and Kuzma [39] that shows the following: every nn-vertex graph XX with at least two vertices of degree n−1n-1 is realizable as the commuting graph of a semigroup. It is easy to see that their construction actually gives a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a semigroup with nn elements and a bijection from it to the vertex set of XX such that the edges of XX realize the commuting relation of the semigroup. It is a nearly complete answer to the question in the semigroups setting.

Solomon and Woldar [74] have shown that the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) of a finite simple group GG uniquely determines the group. More precisely, they have shown that for any finite group HH and any finite simple group GG, their commuting graphs Γ⁡(H)\Gamma(H) and Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) are isomorphic if and only if the groups GG and HH are isomorphic. An interesting question is whether or not the proof of this result [74] yields a polynomial-time algorithm for checking if a given graph XX is the commuting graph of a simple group.

4 Basic properties

We being with some preliminary observations that are well-known in the literature (see, e.g., the survey [22]).

Let GG be a finite group. We first describe the cliques of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). If a vertex subset SS induces a clique in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) then SS is a commuting subset of elements of GG. Conversely, every commuting subset of elements of GG forms a clique in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). Which cliques of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) correspond to subgroups of GG? Although we cannot directly infer the group multiplication from Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), we can observe the following.

Lemma 4.1

Let GG be a finite group and Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) its commuting graph. A vertex subset SS is a maximal clique of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) if and only if SS is a maximal abelian subgroup of GG.

Proof 3

Suppose HH is a maximal abelian subgroup of GG. Clearly, HH is a clique in XX. If x∉Hx\notin H is adjacent to all of HH then xx commutes with each element of HH implying that ⟨H∪{x}⟩\langle H\cup\{x\}\rangle is an abelian subgroup of GG strictly larger than HH. Hence the clique induced by HH is maximal.

Conversely, suppose S⊂GS\subset G is a maximal clique in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). Then any two elements x,y∈Sx,y\in S commute with each other. Hence, the subgroup H=⟨S⟩H=\langle S\rangle generated by SS is an abelian subgroup of GG which means that the vertex subset consisting of elements of HH is a clique in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) containing SS. As SS is maximal, by assumption, it follows that S=HS=H which means SS is a maximal abelian subgroup. ∎

4.1 The vertex degrees of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) and conjugacy classes of GG

Let X=(G,E)X=(G,E) be the commuting graph of a finite group GG. Let xGx^{G} denote the conjugacy class of x∈Gx\in G:

xG={g−1​x​g∣g∈G},x^{G}=\{g^{-1}xg\mid g\in G\},

which is the orbit of xx under the conjugation action of GG on itself. Let deg⁡(v)\deg(v) denote the degree of a vertex vv in the graph XX. The orbit-stabilizer lemma [20] directly implies the following.

Proposition 4.2

For each x∈Gx\in G its centralizer CG​(x)C_{G}(x) is the closed neighborhood N¯​(x)\bar{N}(x) of xx in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), and

|CG​(x)|=1+deg⁡(x)=|G||xG|, for all ​x∈G.|C_{G}(x)|=1+\deg(x)={\frac{|G|}{|x^{G}|}},\textrm{ for all }x\in G.

Let n=|G|n=|G|, let mm denote the number of edges in the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), and let kk denote the number of conjugacy classes. As ∑x∈Gdeg⁡(x)=2​m\sum_{x\in G}\deg(x)=2m, we have:

2​m+n=∑x∈G|G||xG|=|G|⋅∑x∈G1|xG|=n⋅k.2m+n=\sum_{x\in G}{\frac{|G|}{|x^{G}|}}=|G|\cdot\sum_{x\in G}{\frac{1}{|x^{G}|}}=n\cdot k. (6)

Thus the number of conjugacy classes of GG is k=(2​m+n)/nk=(2m+n)/n, which, by the above equation, can be inferred from the commuting graph. Thus, for example, the only regular commuting graphs are the complete graphs, which are the commuting graphs of abelian groups.

Let f⁡(n)f(n) denote the minimum number of conjugacy classes in a group of order nn. The function f⁡(n)f(n) is quite well studied. Landau [53] showed that f⁡(n)→∞f(n)\to\infty as n→∞n\to\infty. The first lower bound was obtained by Brauer [11] and Erdős and Turán [35], who showed that f⁡(n)≥log⁡log⁡nf(n)\geq\log\log n (logarithms to base 22). This was improved to ϵ​log⁡n/(log⁡log⁡n)8\epsilon\log n/(\log\log n)^{8} by Pyber [65]. The exponent 88 in the previous expression was reduced to 77 by Keller [50], and then to 3+ϵ3+\epsilon by Baumeister, Maróti and Tong-Viet [8], for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0. It is conjectured that a bound of the form f⁡(n)≥C​log⁡nf(n)\geq C\log n holds for some constant CC.

This is relevant to the recognition problem because of the following observation, which follows immediately from equation (6).

Proposition 4.3

An nn-vertex graph XX with fewer than n⁡(f⁡(n)−1)2\frac{n(f(n)-1)}{2} edges cannot be the commuting graph of a group, where f⁡(n)f(n) is the minimum number of conjugacy classes that a group of order nn can have.

At the other extreme, we can rule out very dense incomplete graphs by the 5/85/8-theorem [44] for finite groups. More precisely, for any finite non-abelian group GG with nn elements:

|C|=|{(x,y)∣x,y∈G and xy=yx}|≤58⋅n2,|C|=|\{(x,y)\mid x,y\in G\textrm{ and }xy=yx\}|\leq\frac{5}{8}\cdot n^{2},

where C⊂G×GC\subset G\times G denotes the set of ordered pairs (x,y)(x,y) of commuting elements. Then, in the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)=(G,E)\Gamma(G)=(G,E) the number of edges

|E|=|C|−n2≤516⋅n2−n2≤58⋅(n2).|E|=\frac{|C|-n}{2}\leq\frac{5}{16}\cdot n^{2}-\frac{n}{2}\leq\frac{5}{8}\cdot{n\choose 2}.

Putting it together, we have:

Proposition 4.4

An incomplete graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) cannot be the commuting graph of a group if |E|>58⋅(|V|2)|E|>\frac{5}{8}\cdot{|V|\choose 2}.

4.2 The commuting graph and maximal abelian subgroups

For a finite group GG, let 2G2^{G} denote its power set and let ℳ⊆2G\mathcal{M}\subseteq 2^{G} denote the set of all maximal abelian subgroups of GG. Associated with GG is the natural hypergraph (G,ℳ)(G,\mathcal{M}), where the hyperedges are precisely the maximal abelian subgroups of GG.

Proposition 4.5

The commuting graph of a finite group determines the hypergraph of its maximal abelian subgroups, and, conversely the maximal abelian subgroups hypergraph of the group determines its commuting graph.

Proof 4

Let GG be a finite group. The maximal abelian subgroups are the maximal cliques in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G); and the edges of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) are the 22-element subsets of maximal abelian subgroups.∎

Remark 1

Since the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) of a finite simple group GG uniquely determines the group [74], by Proposition 4.5 it follows that the set of maximal abelian groups of a finite simple group GG uniquely determines GG.

For a finite group GG, the number of maximal abelian subgroups is bounded by (|G|log⁡|G|){|G|}\choose{\log|G|} because every subgroup of GG has a generating set of size bounded by log⁡|G|\log|G|. This simple bound is tight apart from a constant in the exponent. To see this, consider the extraspecial group GG of order p2​n+1p^{2n+1} and exponent pp, where pp is an odd prime. The centre has order pp, and G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G) is isomorphic to a 2​n2n-dimensional vector space VV over the field FF of pp elements, with the bilinear form from V×VV\times V to FF corresponding to the commutation map from G/Z⁡(G)×G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G)\times G/Z(G) to Z⁡(G)Z(G). Maximal abelian subgroups contain the centre, and correspond to maximal totally isotropic subspaces of VV. It is known that the number of such subspaces is ∏i=1n(pi+1)\prod_{i=1}^{n}(p^{i}+1) (see [78]). As

∏i=1n(pi+1)>pn⁡(n+1)/2>pn⁡(2​n+1)/4=|G|n/4,\prod_{i=1}^{n}(p^{i}+1)>p^{n(n+1)/2}>p^{n(2n+1)/4}=|G|^{n/4},

it follows that the number of maximal abelian subgroups of the extraspecial pp-group GG is |G|Ω⁡(log⁡|G|)|G|^{\Omega(\log|G|)} for any odd prime pp.

5 Commuting graphs of product groups

A natural approach to the problem of recognizing commuting graphs is to examine the connection between product decompositions of the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) and the direct product decomposition of the group GG.

Let GG and HH be finite groups. Consider the commuting graph Γ⁡(G×H)\Gamma(G\times H) of their direct product. We recall the definition of strong products of graphs.

Definition 1

[45, Chapter 4, Page 35] Let X=(V,E)X=(V,E) and X′=(V′,E′)X^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) be simple undirected graphs. Their strong product, denoted X⊠X′X\boxtimes X^{\prime}, is a simple undirected graph with the cartesian product V×V′V\times V^{\prime} as its vertex set and edges defined as follows: distinct pairs (u,u′)(u,u^{\prime}) and (v,v′)(v,v^{\prime}) are adjacent if and only if one of the following holds:

  • (a)

    u=vu=v and (u′,v′)∈E′(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})\in E^{\prime},

  • (b)

    u′=v′u^{\prime}=v^{\prime} and (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E,

  • (c)

    (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E and (u′,v′)∈E′(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})\in E^{\prime}.

The following proposition is immediate from the definition.

Proposition 5.1

For finite groups GG and HH

Γ⁡(G×H)=Γ⁡(G)⊠Γ⁡(H).\Gamma(G\times H)=\Gamma(G)\boxtimes\Gamma(H).

The strong product is both commutative and associative [45, Chapter 4], in the sense that X⊠Y≅Y⊠XX\boxtimes Y\cong Y\boxtimes X and (X⊠Y)⊠Z≅X⊠(Y⊠Z)(X\boxtimes Y)\boxtimes Z\cong X\boxtimes(Y\boxtimes Z).

By a non-trivial graph we mean a graph with more than one vertex. Given a graph XX, a factorization X≅Y⊠ZX\cong Y\boxtimes Z is non-trivial if both YY and ZZ are non-trivial. A graph XX is said to be a prime graph if it does not have a non-trivial factorization. (We warn the reader that this term is also used for graphs defined by arithmetic parameters of a finite group; see for example [57].)

It turns out that any connected graph XX has a unique factorization (up to isomorphism) into a strong product of prime graphs [45, Theorem 7.14]. Moreover, this prime factorization can be computed in polynomial time [36]. As a consequence, we obtain the following polynomial-time reduction.

Recall a group GG is said to be indecomposable if it cannot be expressed as the direct product of two non-trivial groups.

Theorem 5.2

The problem of recognizing the commuting graphs of groups is polynomial-time reducible to the problem of recognizing the commuting graphs of indecomposable groups.

Proof 5

Suppose we have an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for recognizing the commuting graphs of indecomposable groups. Using 𝒜\mathcal{A} as subroutine, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for recognizing the commuting graphs of all finite groups.

Let X=(V,E)X=(V,E) be an undirected graph on nn vertices which is a purported commuting graph.

First, using the polynomial-time algorithm of Feigenbaum and Schäffer [36] we can factorize XX as

X=X1⊠X2⊠⋯⊠Xk,X=X_{1}\boxtimes X_{2}\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes X_{k},

where each XiX_{i} is a prime graph on at least two vertices. It follows that k≤log⁡nk\leq\log n. Now, for each subset S⊆[k]S\subseteq[k] of the prime graphs we combine them by taking the strong direct product to define the graph

XS=⊠i∈SXi.X_{S}=\boxtimes_{i\in S}X_{i}.

Notice that any order in which the strong product of these graphs XiX_{i} is computed yields the same graph, up to isomorphism.

Thus, in time which is polynomial in nn, we have computed graphs XSX_{S} for each subset SS of [k][k]. Now, we invoke the subroutine 𝒜\mathcal{A} that checks if XSX_{S} is the commuting graph of an indecomposable group GSG_{S}, and if so, finds a labeling of the vertices of XSX_{S} with elements of GSG_{S} consistent with the commuting relations.

We can now check if the input graph XX is the commuting graph of a group with a straightforward dynamic programming strategy based on the following claim which directly follows from Proposition 5.1.

Claim 5.3

For any two disjoint subsets S,S′S,S^{\prime} of [k][k] such that XSX_{S} and XS′X_{S^{\prime}} are the commuting graphs of groups GSG_{S} and GS′G_{S^{\prime}} the graph XS⊠XS′X_{S}\boxtimes X_{S^{\prime}} is the commuting graph of the direct product group GS×GS′G_{S}\times G_{S^{\prime}}.

Now, the algorithm works in stages, computing subsets SS of [k][k] along with the graph XSX_{S} and group GSG_{S} such that XS=Γ⁡(GS)X_{S}=\Gamma(G_{S}).

  1. (a)

    for stages 00 to kk do

  2. (b)

    Stage 00   we have subsets SS such that GSG_{S} is an indecomposable group. We mark all such subsets SS as true. We mark the remaining subsets as false.

  3. (c)

    Stage i+1i+1   For each pair of disjoint subsets SS and S′S^{\prime} marked true in Stages 1,2,…,i1,2,\ldots,i, such that S∪S′S\cup S^{\prime} is marked false, we mark S∪S′S\cup S^{\prime} true and compute XS∪S′=XS⊠XS′X_{S\cup S^{\prime}}=X_{S}\boxtimes X_{S^{\prime}} and GS∪S′=GS×GS′G_{S\cup S^{\prime}}=G_{S}\times G_{S^{\prime}}.

  4. (d)

    end-for

  5. (e)

    If [k][k] is marked true then the input XX is the commuting graph of the group G[k]G_{[k]} computed above.

The above description checks if XX is the commuting graph of a group with at most 2k≤n2^{k}\leq n calls to the subroutine 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the running time of the remaining computation is clearly polynomially bounded in nn.∎

As mentioned in the introduction, the Solomon–Woldar theorem [74] shows that the commuting graph of a finite simple group uniquely determines it. Let the group G=G1×G2×⋯×GtG=G_{1}\times G_{2}\times\cdots\times G_{t} be the direct product of finite simple groups Gi,1≤i≤tG_{i},1\leq i\leq t. By Proposition 5.1 we can express its commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) as

Γ(G)=Γ(G1)×Γ(G2)×⋯×Γ(Gt)\Gamma(G)=\Gamma(G_{1})\times\Gamma(G_{2})\times\cdots\times\Gamma(G_{t})

using the strong product. Putting it together, we can deduce the following.

Corollary 5.4

If GG is a direct product of simple groups, then GG is uniquely determined by its commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G).

We do not know if the commuting graph of an indecomposable group GG is necessarily a prime graph. However, if GG is simple then it turns out, as we show below, that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a prime graph.

Lemma 5.5

The commuting graph of a finite simple group is a prime graph under the strong product.

Proof 6

We use the fact that, if GG is a non-abelian simple group and g∈G∖{1}g\in G\setminus\{1\}, then there exists h∈Gh\in G such that ⟨g,h⟩=G\langle g,h\rangle=G [43]. Now if ⟨g,h⟩=G\langle g,h\rangle=G, then

  • (a)

    gg and hh are nonadjacent in the commuting graph (since GG is non-abelian);

  • (b)

    gg and hh have no non-identity common neighbour in the commuting graph (since a common neighbour would belong to Z⁡(G)Z(G), but Z⁡(G)={1}Z(G)=\{1\}.

Now suppose for a contradiction that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is the strong product of two non-trivial graphs with vertex sets AA and BB (i.e., with |A|>1|A|>1 and |B|>1|B|>1). Then we can identify GG, as the vertex set of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), with the Cartesian product A×BA\times B. Suppose that (a,b)(a,b) is the identity of GG. Then (a,b)(a,b) is joined to all other vertices in the commuting graph.

It follows that aa is joined to every other vertex in AA, and bb to every other vertex in BB; therefore, for all x∈A∖{a}x\in A\setminus\{a\}, y∈B∖{b}y\in B\setminus\{b\}, the three vertices (a,y)(a,y), (x,b)(x,b) and (x,y)(x,y) are adjacent to each other in the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G).

Choose y∈B∖{b}y\in B\setminus\{b\}, and suppose that ⟨(a,y),(u,v)⟩=G\langle(a,y),(u,v)\rangle=G. Now

  • (a)

    if u=au=a then (a,y)(a,y) and (a,v)(a,v) are both joined to (x,b)(x,b) for any x∈A∖{a}x\in A\setminus\{a\};

  • (b)

    if v=bv=b then (a,y)(a,y) and (u,b)(u,b) are joined;

  • (c)

    if neither of the above, then (a,y)(a,y) and (u,v)(u,v) are both joined to (u,b)(u,b).

Each case is contradictory; so our assumption that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is the strong product of two non-trivial graphs is false, and the theorem is proved.∎

Remark 2

The proof of Lemma 5.5 only requires that Z⁡(G)=1Z(G)=1 and that any non-identity element is contained in a 22-element generating set. These assumptions are valid in any almost simple group GG with simple normal subgroup SS such that G/SG/S is cyclic [18].

As a consequence of Lemma 5.5, we obtain the following variant of Theorem 5.2.

Theorem 5.6

The problem of recognizing the commuting graph of a direct product of simple groups is polynomial-time reducible to the problem of recognizing the commuting graph of a simple group.

The algorithm for the reduction in the above theorem is much simpler and more efficient than in Theorem 5.2. For we only need to consider the prime factors XiX_{i}, in the factorization X=⊠i=1kXiX=\boxtimes_{i=1}^{k}X_{i}, and not all the strong products XSX_{S} for arbitrary subsets S⊆[k]S\subseteq[k].

6 Commuting graphs of semidirect products

In this section we explore whether we can recognize the commuting graphs of semidirect products G=H⋊KG=H\rtimes K if HH and KK are both from group classes whose commuting graphs are easily recognizable.

For example, consider the commuting graph of the dihedral group D2​nD_{2n}. Let D2​n=⟨a,b⟩D_{2n}=\langle a,b\rangle where an=b2=1a^{n}=b^{2}=1 and b​a​b=a−1bab=a^{-1}. For nn odd, 11 is the only dominating vertex, there is an nn-clique corresponding to ⟨a⟩\langle a\rangle and the b​aiba^{i} correspond to pendant vertices. Thus, the commuting graph of D2​nD_{2n} is easily recognizable. For nn even, it is a bit different with an/2a^{n/2} being the other dominating vertex.

More generally, consider the generalized dihedral group ⟨A,t⟩\langle A,t\rangle defined earlier, where AA is abelian of order 2​n2n, nn odd. Its commuting graph is isomorphic to that of the dihedral group D2​nD_{2n} of the same order. Hence, as observed above, we can recognize that a graph is the commuting graph of a generalized dihedral group, but cannot decide which one.

Seeking a generalization of this example we consider Frobenius groups.

6.1 Commuting graphs of Frobenius groups

In this subsection we demonstrate that we can recognise from its commuting graph that a group GG is a Frobenius group. These groups were defined earlier. Let GG be a Frobenius group with kernel NN and complement HH.

Thompson [79] proved that the Frobenius kernel is nilpotent, and Zassenhaus [84] worked out the detailed structure of a Frobenius complement. Everything we need about Frobenius groups is explained in standard group theory texts  [63, 46, 72].

In the commuting graph of a group GG, the identity is a dominating vertex (that is, joined to all others); indeed, any vertex in the centre is dominating, so if Z⁡(G)Z(G) is non-trivial then the commuting graph is 22-connected.

Lemma 6.1
  1. (a)

    A Frobenius kernel has non-trivial centre.

  2. (b)

    A Frobenius complement has non-trivial centre.

Proof 7

(a) By Thompson’s theorem [79, Theorem 1], a Frobenius kernel is nilpotent, and nilpotent groups have a non-trivial centre.

(b) Let HH be a Frobenius complement. By [46, Theorem 6.3, Corollary 6.10], if HH has even order, then it has a unique element of order 22, which lies in the centre; while, if HH has odd order, then it has a unique subgroup of order pp for every pp dividing |H||H|. In the latter case, choose pp to be the smallest prime divisor of HH, and P=⟨a⟩P=\langle a\rangle the unique subgroup of order pp. Then PP is a normal subgroup of HH. For any h∈Hh\in H, we have ah=ama^{h}=a^{m} for some mm with 1≤m≤p−11\leq m\leq p-1. If m>1m>1, let qq be a prime divisor of mm; then some power of hh has order qq, a contradiction. So ah=aa^{h}=a for all h∈Hh\in H, whence a∈Z⁡(H)a\in Z(H).∎

Theorem 6.2

Let GG be a group of order n​knk, where n>1n>1, k>1k>1, and nn and kk are relatively prime. Then GG is a Frobenius group with Frobenius complement of order kk if and only if its commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) satisfies the following conditions:

  • (a)

    there is a unique dominating vertex 11 in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), where 11 corresponds to the identity element of GG.

  • (b)

    Γ⁡(G)∖{1}\Gamma(G)\setminus\{1\} has a component of size n−1n-1 and nn components of size k−1k-1, and each component has a dominating vertex.

Proof 8

Let GG be a group of order n​k,n>1,k>1nk,n>1,k>1 with nn and kk relatively prime.

We prove the forward direction first. Suppose that GG is a Frobenius group with Frobenius complement HH of order kk and Frobenius kernel NN. Then, as G=N⋊HG=N\rtimes H, |G|=|N|⋅|H||G|=|N|\cdot|H| which implies the kernel NN is of order nn. Consider the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). As the identity element commutes with every other element in GG, it is a dominating vertex in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). We recall [3, 35.24 and 35.25] that N​⊴​GN\trianglelefteq G, CG​(h)≤HC_{G}(h)\leq H for each h∈Hh\in H, and CG​(x)≤NC_{G}(x)\leq N for each x∈N∖{1}x\in N\setminus\{1\}. Therefore, non-identity vertices in NN do not commute with non-identity vertices in a complement. Thus the identity element is the unique dominating vertex in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). Moreover, non-identity vertices in different complements do not commute with each other. Thus the components of Γ⁡(G)∖{1}\Gamma(G)\setminus\{1\} are as stated, and Lemma 6.1 shows that they have dominating vertices.

Conversely, suppose that the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) has properties (a) and (b). If CC is a component with a dominating vertex cc, then the centralizer CG​(c)C_{G}(c) is equal to C∪{1}C\cup\{1\}, which is thus a subgroup of GG. Let NN be the subgroup containing the component of size n−1n-1, and let H1,…,HnH_{1},\ldots,H_{n} be the subgroups containing the other components. Note that |N|=n|N|=n and |Hi|=k,1≤i≤n|H_{i}|=k,1\leq i\leq n.

Since Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is invariant under automorphisms of GG, we have an action of GG on the set Ω\Omega of components of Γ⁡(G)∖{1}\Gamma(G)\setminus\{1\} of size k−1k-1 by conjugation. We show that this action satisfies the conditions for a Frobenius group given above.

Choose a prime pp dividing kk. Since nn and kk are relatively prime, pp does not divide nn. So the subgroup NN cannot contain a Sylow pp-subgroup; but each of H1,…,HnH_{1},\ldots,H_{n} contains such a subgroup. By the conjugacy part of Sylow’s theorem, GG acts transitively on Ω\Omega.

For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, each element of Hi∖{1}H_{i}\setminus\{1\} acting by conjugation, fixes itself and so fixes the component induced by Hi∖{1}H_{i}\setminus\{1\}. That is, a non-identity element of G∖NG\setminus N, acting by conjugation, fixes itself, and so fixes the component containing it. We must show that it fixes no other component. To that end, we count the fixed points of elements of GG acting on Ω\Omega. The identity fixes nn; each non-identity element of NN fixes some non-negative number; and each of the remaining elements G∖NG\setminus N fix a positive number of elements. So the sum of the fixed point numbers is at least n+n⁡(k−1)=n​kn+n(k-1)=nk. But, by the Orbit-Counting Lemma, this sum is equal to |G|=n​k|G|=nk, since GG is transitive. Consequently, non-identity elements of NN do not fix any point of Ω\Omega, and the remaining non-identity elements fix exactly one point each. So GG is a Frobenius group.∎

Suppose XX is a graph given as input such that X=Γ⁡(G)X=\Gamma(G) for some group GG. Then Theorem 6.2 gives us a polynomial-time test for checking if the group GG is a Frobenius group.

Remark 3

Above we assumed that our graph is a commuting graph. However, it is easy to construct a graph satisfying the conditions of Theorem 6.2 which is not a commuting graph. Can we find necessary and sufficient conditions for Γ\Gamma to be the commuting graph of a Frobenius group?

7 Recognizing commuting graphs of extraspecial groups

In this section we design a polynomial-time algorithm that takes a simple undirected graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E), with n=p2​r+1n=p^{2r+1} vertices, r≥2r\geq 2 and pp an odd prime, as input and determines if XX is the commuting graph of an extraspecial group GG of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1} (see Section 2 for definition). The algorithm will also compute a certifying bijection v↦gvv\mapsto g_{v} labeling each vertex v∈Vv\in V by a unique group element gv∈Gg_{v}\in G such that the commuting relations hold.

There are exactly two non-isomorphic extraspecial groups of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, for each r≥1r\geq 1 and each prime pp. These two groups, which we denote as G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, are described below.

  • (a)

    The first group G1G_{1} is generated by 2​r+12r+1 elements G1=⟨z,xi,yi,1≤i≤r⟩G_{1}=\langle z,x_{i},y_{i},1\leq i\leq r\rangle such that [xi,xj]=1[x_{i},x_{j}]=1, [yi,yj]=1[y_{i},y_{j}]=1 for all i,ji,j, and [xi,yj]=1[x_{i},y_{j}]=1 for all i≠ji\neq j, [xi,yi]=z[x_{i},y_{i}]=z for all ii, and xip=yip=zp=1x_{i}^{p}=y_{i}^{p}=z^{p}=1 for all ii. The centre Z⁡(G1)=⟨z⟩Z(G_{1})=\langle z\rangle.

  • (b)

    The second group G2G_{2} also has 2​r+12r+1 generators G2=⟨z,xi,yi,1≤i≤r⟩G_{2}=\langle z,x_{i},y_{i},1\leq i\leq r\rangle such that [xi,xj]=1[x_{i},x_{j}]=1, [yi,yj]=1[y_{i},y_{j}]=1 for all i,ji,j, and [xi,yj]=1[x_{i},y_{j}]=1 for all i≠ji\neq j. And [xi,yi]=z[x_{i},y_{i}]=z for all ii, and xip=1=zpx_{i}^{p}=1=z^{p}, yip=zy_{i}^{p}=z for all ii. The centre Z⁡(G2)=⟨z⟩Z(G_{2})=\langle z\rangle.

Each element g∈G1∖{1}g\in G_{1}\setminus\{1\} has order pp. On the other hand, each element g∈G2∖{1}g\in G_{2}\setminus\{1\} has order either pp or p2p^{2}. Hence, G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} are non-isomorphic. We refer to Gorenstein [41, Chapter 5] for more about extraspecial groups.

We now analyze the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) for G∈{G1,G2}G\in\{G_{1},G_{2}\} of order n=p2​r+1n=p^{2r+1}. The vertices of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) corresponding to the centre Z⁡(G)=Z=⟨z⟩Z(G)=Z=\langle z\rangle are precisely the pp vertices of degree p2​r+1−1p^{2r+1}-1 each. In either case (G∈{G1,G2}G\in\{G_{1},G_{2}\}) we have:

  • (a)

    The quotient group G/ZG/Z is an elementary abelian pp-group of order p2​rp^{2r}.

  • (b)

    The centre ZZ can be identified with the finite field 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and G/ZG/Z can be identified with the 2​r2r-dimensional vector space V⁡(2​r,p)=𝔽p2​rV(2r,p)=\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2r}.

Furthermore, as Z=G′Z=G^{\prime}, for x,y∈Gx,y\in G we can write their commutator [x,y]=zix,y[x,y]=z^{i_{x,y}} for some 0≤ix,y≤p−10\leq i_{x,y}\leq p-1. Hence, the commutation map

(x​Z​(G),y​Z​(G))↦[x,y](xZ(G),yZ(G))\mapsto[x,y]

from G/Z×G/Z→ZG/Z\times G/Z\to Z can be identified with a bilinear form ⟨,⟩:V(2r,p)×V(2r,p)→𝔽p\langle,\rangle:V(2r,p)\times V(2r,p)\to\mathbb{F}_{p} that satisfies the following:

  • (a)

    It is symplectic: We have ⟨x,y⟩=−⟨y,x⟩\langle x,y\rangle=-\langle y,x\rangle for all x,y∈V⁡(2​r,p)x,y\in V(2r,p). In particular, ⟨x,x⟩=0\langle x,x\rangle=0 for all x∈V⁡(2​r,p)x\in V(2r,p).

  • (b)

    It is non-degenerate: there is no non-zero u∈V⁡(2​r,p)u\in V(2r,p) such that ⟨u,v⟩=0\langle u,v\rangle=0 for all v∈V⁡(2​r,p)v\in V(2r,p).

Definition 2

The vector space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) equipped with a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle is a symplectic space.

If ⟨u,v⟩=0\langle u,v\rangle=0 we say uu is orthogonal to vv. For a subset SS of the symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) let

S⟂={u∈V⁡(2​r,p)∣⟨u,v⟩=0​ for all ​v∈S}S^{\perp}=\{u\in V(2r,p)\mid\langle u,v\rangle=0\text{ for all }v\in S\}

denote the subspace of V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) consisting of vectors orthogonal to each vector in SS.

Definition 3

A symplectic basis for the symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) is a basis of 2​r2r vectors x¯i,y¯i,1≤i≤r\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i},1\leq i\leq r such that:

  • (a)

    ⟨x¯i,y¯i⟩=1\langle\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i}\rangle=1 for all ii.

  • (b)

    ⟨x¯i,y¯j⟩=0\langle\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{j}\rangle=0 for all i≠ji\neq j.

  • (c)

    ⟨x¯i,x¯j⟩=0\langle\bar{x}_{i},\bar{x}_{j}\rangle=0 for all i,ji,j.

  • (d)

    ⟨y¯i,y¯j⟩=0\langle\bar{y}_{i},\bar{y}_{j}\rangle=0 for all i,ji,j.

The symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) has a symplectic basis [83, Section 3.4.4].

Remark 4

We will describe an elementary self-contained polynomial-time algorithm for recognising commuting graphs of extraspecial groups. We have an alternative algorithm, based on the Buekenhout-Shult theorem [17] classifying certain point-line geometries, that exploits the finite geometry structure of the quotient group G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G). However, we present the former in the interest of keeping the proof entirely self-contained in the context of this paper.

Lemma 7.1

Given as input the multiplication table of an extraspecial group GG of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, in time polynomial in p2​r+1p^{2r+1} we can construct its associated symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle, as an explicit bilinear map from 𝔽p2​r×𝔽p2​r→𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2r}\times\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2r}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}.

Proof 9

Let n=p2​r+1n=p^{2r+1}. First, we compute the centre Z=⟨z⟩Z=\langle z\rangle of GG from the multiplication table. In order to compute G/ZG/Z we can find its multiplication table from the given multiplication table of GG. We can find a decomposition of G/ZG/Z as the direct product of 2​r2r cyclic groups of order pp by finding independent generators for G/ZG/Z using a simple algorithm. Suppose g1,g2,…,gj∈G/Zg_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{j}\in G/Z are independent (i.e. the identity can be expressed as a product of their powers only if the exponents are all zero). If j<2​rj<2r then the subgroup Hj=⟨g1,g2,…,gj⟩H_{j}=\langle g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{j}\rangle which is of size pjp^{j} can be listed in time polynomial in nn. We can pick gj+1g_{j+1} as any element in G∖HjG\setminus H_{j} and continue the process until we pick 2​r2r such independent generators which will generate G/ZG/Z. That gives us an efficient identification of G/ZG/Z with V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p). For x​Z,y​Z∈G/ZxZ,yZ\in G/Z we will have corresponding vectors vx,vy∈V⁡(2​r,p)v_{x},v_{y}\in V(2r,p). If the commutator [x,y]=zix,y[x,y]=z^{i_{x,y}} then we can define the symplectic form as ⟨vx,vy⟩=ix,y\langle v_{x},v_{y}\rangle=i_{x,y}, where ix,y∈𝔽pi_{x,y}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}. This completes the proof. ∎

Definition 4

The symplectic graph of the symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) (equipped with symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle) is an undirected simple graph with V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) as vertex set such that for each pair of distinct vectors u,v∈V⁡(2​r,p)u,v\in V(2r,p), (u,v)(u,v) is an undirected edge in the graph precisely when ⟨u,v⟩=0\langle u,v\rangle=0.

In particular, let S1S_{1} and S2S_{2} denote the associated symplectic graphs of the two extraspecial groups G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, respectively.

Lemma 7.2
  1. (a)

    The commuting graphs Γ⁡(G1)\Gamma(G_{1}) and Γ⁡(G2)\Gamma(G_{2}) are isomorphic.

  2. (b)

    The associated symplectic graphs S1S_{1} and S2S_{2} are isomorphic.

Recall, as defined at the beginning of this section, that both G1=⟨x1,x2,…,xr,y1,y2,…,yr,z⟩G_{1}=\langle x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{r},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{r},z\rangle and G2=⟨x1,x2,…,xr,y1,y2,…,yr,z⟩G_{2}=\langle x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{r},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{r},z\rangle. Let V1V_{1} and V2V_{2} denote the symplectic spaces corresponding to the groups G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, respectively. We now show that the symplectic graph of an extraspecial group GG can be computed in polynomial time, given just its commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) as input.

Lemma 7.3

Given as input the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), of an extraspecial group GG of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, pp an odd prime, we can compute in polynomial time an undirected graph Xs=(Vs,Es)X_{s}=(V_{s},E_{s}) with |Vs|=p2​r|V_{s}|=p^{2r} such that XsX_{s} is the symplectic graph associated with GG.

7.1 Recognizing the symplectic graph

We now show that the symplectic graph of a non-degenerate symplectic form on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) can be recognized in polynomial time.

Theorem 7.6

Given a simple undirected graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) on a vertex set VV of size p2​rp^{2r}, for an odd prime pp, in time polynomial in the size of XX we can recognize if XX is the associated symplectic graph of an extraspecial group of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}. Furthermore, the algorithm will also compute a bijection from VV to V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) and determine an associated symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle.

Proof 12

The somewhat detailed proof is structured as a series of claims followed by a description of the algorithm and its analysis.

Let X=(V,E)X=(V,E) be a graph with p2​rp^{2r} vertices. Our algorithm will be recursive, with correctness proof based on an inductive argument. We know that the symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) has a symplectic basis of 2​r2r vectors of the form x¯i,y¯i,1≤i≤r\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i},1\leq i\leq r as defined in Definition 3.

We first note that given a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p), we can construct a symplectic basis for V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) with the following greedy procedure.

  • (a)

    Pick x¯1≠0\bar{x}_{1}\neq 0 in V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) arbitrarily.

  • (b)

    Since ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle is non-degenerate, we can find a vector u¯∈V⁡(2​r,p)\bar{u}\in V(2r,p) such that ⟨x¯1,u¯⟩=α≠0\langle\bar{x}_{1},\bar{u}\rangle=\alpha\neq 0. Define y¯1=α−1​u¯\bar{y}_{1}=\alpha^{-1}\bar{u} such that ⟨x¯1,y¯1⟩=1\langle\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}\rangle=1.

  • (c)

    Then notice that the subspace {x¯1,y¯1}⟂\{\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}\}^{\perp} is a 2​r−22r-2 dimensional symplectic space V′V^{\prime} (w.r.t. the same symplectic form). We can continue with the basis construction, recursively applying the above two steps to V′V^{\prime}.

Now, suppose X=(V,E)X=(V,E) is the graph given as input on p2​rp^{2r} vertices. If XX is indeed the symplectic graph of V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) for some symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle, we will describe a polynomial-time recursive procedure that recovers a bijection from VV to V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) along with a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle as witness for XX being the associated symplectic graph. We will then argue that if XX is not a symplectic graph then this procedure detects that.

Essentially, the problem is to efficiently simulate the above two-step basis construction procedure given only the graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) as input. As the symplectic space is non-degenerate, the zero vector 00 is the only vertex in XX adjacent to all others and is easily identified. Let x1x_{1} be any other vertex in VV and we choose a non-zero vector x¯1∈V⁡(2​r,p)\bar{x}_{1}\in V(2r,p) as its image. Next, we will choose y1y_{1} as any vertex not adjacent to x1x_{1} in the graph XX and choose a non-zero vector y¯1∈V⁡(2​r,p)\bar{y}_{1}\in V(2r,p) as its image. Let

V′={v∈V∣(v,x1)∈E​ and ​(v,y1)∈E}.V^{\prime}=\{v\in V\mid(v,x_{1})\in E\text{ and }(v,y_{1})\in E\}.

That is, V′V^{\prime} is the common neighborhood of x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}. We can easily identify V′V^{\prime} in XX. Let X′X^{\prime} be the subgraph of XX induced by the vertex subset V′V^{\prime}. We have the following simple observation.

Claim 7.7

If XX is the symplectic graph of a 2​r2r-dimensional symplectic space over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} then the graph X′X^{\prime} is the symplectic graph of a symplectic space of dimension 2​r−22r-2 over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}.

The algorithm will now recursively check that X′X^{\prime} is indeed the symplectic graph of a 2​r−22r-2-dimensional symplectic space V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. If so, it will compute a labeling of the vertices of V′V^{\prime} by linear combinations ∑i=2r(αi​x¯i+βi​y¯i),αi,βi∈𝔽p\sum_{i=2}^{r}(\alpha_{i}\bar{x}_{i}+\beta_{i}\bar{y}_{i}),\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p} that is consistent with the orthogonality relation of a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle. Here the basis vectors computed by the algorithm are x¯i,y¯i\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i} for 2≤i≤r2\leq i\leq r. At the end of the recursive call, the algorithm computes a bijection from V′V^{\prime} to V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) that labels each vertex in V′V^{\prime} by a distinct linear combination of the basis vectors.

Now, the remaining task for the algorithm is to find a labeling of the vertices in V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} consistent with a symplectic form on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p), assuming XX is a symplectic graph.

For each vertex vv we will denote its vector label by v¯\bar{v}. For a labeled subset SS of vertices of VV we will use S¯⊆V⁡(2​r,p)\bar{S}\subseteq V(2r,p) to denote the set of vectors labeling vertices in SS.

Claim 7.8

A vertex v∈V∖V′v\in V\setminus V^{\prime} can be labeled by a non-zero vector α​x¯1+β​y¯1\alpha\bar{x}_{1}+\beta\bar{y}_{1} in V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p), α,β∈𝔽p\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{p}, if and only if (v,u)∈E(v,u)\in E for all u∈V′u\in V^{\prime}.

Proof of Claim. Consider the symplectic graph of V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p). Let V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) denote the subspace spanned by x¯i,y¯i,2≤i≤n\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i},2\leq i\leq n. Clearly, every vector of the form α​x¯1+β​y¯1,α,β∈𝔽p\alpha\bar{x}_{1}+\beta\bar{y}_{1},\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}_{p} is orthogonal to each vector in V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p).
