Since V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) is non-degenerate, there is a u∈V⁡(2​r−2,p)u\in V(2r-2,p) such that ⟨v,u⟩≠0\langle v,u\rangle\neq 0 which implies ⟨α​x¯1+β​y¯1+v,u⟩=⟨v,u⟩≠0\langle\alpha\bar{x}_{1}+\beta\bar{y}_{1}+v,u\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle\neq 0.

Thus, the algorithm can find a subset V12V_{12} of precisely p2−1p^{2}-1 many such vertices in VV that are adjacent to all of V′V^{\prime}, of which we have already labeled two vertices as x¯1\bar{x}_{1} and y¯1\bar{y}_{1}. We analyze the subgraph X12X_{12} of XX induced by V12V_{12}.

Claim 7.9

The subgraph X12X_{12} induced by V12V_{12} consists of a disjoint union of p+1p+1 many (p−1)(p-1)-size cliques, C1,C2,…,Cp+1C_{1},C_{2},\ldots,C_{p+1}. Furthermore, the labeling procedure must label the vertices of each CiC_{i} from the set {α​u¯∣α∈𝔽p∗}\{\alpha\bar{u}\mid\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{*}_{p}\} of p−1p-1 vectors, for some non-zero vector u¯∈Span(x¯1,y¯1)\bar{u}\in\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}).

Proof of Claim. It is clear from the definition of V12V_{12} that the vertices in it must be labeled by nonzero vectors in Span(x¯1,y¯1)\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}). The proof follows easily by observing that a non-zero vector α​x¯1+β​y¯1\alpha\bar{x}_{1}+\beta\bar{y}_{1} is orthogonal only to itself and its scalar multiples and to no other vectors in Span(x¯1,y¯1)\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}).

By the above claim, we can consistently label each vertex u∈V12u\in V_{12} by a vector u¯∈Span(x¯1,y¯1)\bar{u}\in\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}) assuming XX is a symplectic graph.

Claim 7.10

If X=(V,E)X=(V,E) is the symplectic graph of the symplectic space V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) and V′V^{\prime} corresponds to the symplectic subspace V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) spanned by {x¯i,y¯i∣2≤i≤r}\{\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i}\mid 2\leq i\leq r\} then for any vertex u∈V12u\in V_{12} the vertex subset

V⁡[u]={v∈V∖V′∣(v,u)∈E}V[u]=\{v\in V\setminus V^{\prime}\mid(v,u)\in E\}

has to be labeled by the vectors

{αu¯+v¯∣α≠0,v¯∈Span(∪i=2r{x¯i,y¯i})}\{\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v}\mid\alpha\neq 0,\bar{v}\in\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\cup_{i=2}^{r}\{\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i}\})\}

of V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p).

Proof of Claim. Suppose v∈V∖V′v\in V\setminus V^{\prime} is labeled by the vector a¯+b¯\bar{a}+\bar{b}, where a¯∈Span(x¯1,y¯1)\bar{a}\in\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}) and b¯∈V⁡(2​r−2,p)\bar{b}\in V(2r-2,p). As v∈V⁡[u]v\in V[u] we have

⟨a¯+b¯,u¯⟩=0.\langle\bar{a}+\bar{b},\bar{u}\rangle=0.

As ⟨b¯,u¯⟩=0\langle\bar{b},\bar{u}\rangle=0 it implies that ⟨a¯,u¯⟩=0\langle\bar{a},\bar{u}\rangle=0 which means a¯=α​u¯\bar{a}=\alpha\bar{u} for some non-zero scalar α\alpha. Conversely, any vertex labeled by α​u¯+b¯\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{b} for b¯∈V⁡(2​r−2,p)\bar{b}\in V(2r-2,p) has to lie in V⁡[u]V[u] if the labeling is consistent with the symplectic graph XX.

It follows that |V⁡[u]|=(p−1)⋅p2​r−2|V[u]|=(p-1)\cdot p^{2r-2}. Furthermore, if vertices uu and vv are in the same (p−1)(p-1)-clique in the graph X12X_{12} then V⁡[u]=V⁡[v]V[u]=V[v]. As (p+1)​(p−1)⋅p2​r−2=p2​r−p2​r−2=|V∖V′|(p+1)(p-1)\cdot p^{2r-2}=p^{2r}-p^{2r-2}=|V\setminus V^{\prime}|, it follows that the different V⁡[u]V[u] are all pairwise disjoint and form a partition of V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime}. Consequently, we can identify the p+1p+1 many equisized vertex subsets V⁡[u]V[u] which form a partition of V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime}.

Labelling vertices in V⁡[u]V[u]

By Claim 7.10, the vertices of V⁡[u]V[u] have to be labeled by vectors from {αu¯+v¯∣v∈V′,α≠0}\{\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v}\mid v\in V^{\prime},\alpha\neq 0\}. We will examine the adjacencies in the subgraph induced by V⁡[u]V[u] and also the adjacencies across the different V⁡[u]V[u] and V⁡[u′]V[u^{\prime}] to determine a consistent labeling. Let X⁡[u]X[u] denote the subgraph of XX induced by V⁡[u]V[u].

For distinct vertices v1,v2∈V′v_{1},v_{2}\in V^{\prime} notice that

⟨v¯1,v¯2⟩=⟨α​u¯+v¯1,β​u¯+v¯2⟩.\langle\bar{v}_{1},\bar{v}_{2}\rangle=\langle\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v}_{1},\beta\bar{u}+\bar{v}_{2}\rangle. (7)

Thus, in any consistent labeling of V⁡[u]V[u] suppose Su,vi⊂V⁡[u]S_{u,v_{i}}\subset V[u] are the p−1p-1 vertices labeled by {α​u¯+v¯i∣α≠0}\{\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v}_{i}\mid\alpha\neq 0\} for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Then Equation 7 implies that in the subgraph X⁡[u]X[u] the bipartite graph induced by the subsets Su,v1S_{u,v_{1}} and Su,v2S_{u,v_{2}} is either complete or empty.

Furthermore, ⟨α​u¯+v¯,β​u¯+v¯⟩=0\langle\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v},\beta\bar{u}+\bar{v}\rangle=0 for all non-zero α,β\alpha,\beta. Hence each Su,v,v∈V′S_{u,v},v\in V^{\prime} induces a (p−1)(p-1)-clique.

How do we identify each Su,vS_{u,v}? Suppose v1,v2∈V′v_{1},v_{2}\in V^{\prime} are distinct vertices. In V′V^{\prime} (which is already labeled by V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p)) we can find a vertex v3v_{3} such that ⟨v1,v3⟩≠0\langle v_{1},v_{3}\rangle\neq 0 and ⟨v2,v3⟩=0\langle v_{2},v_{3}\rangle=0. Hence each Su,vS_{u,v} can be identified because

  • (a)

    All p−1p-1 vertices in Su,vS_{u,v} are adjacent to each other. They all have identical neighborhoods in X⁡[u]X[u] by the above argument.

  • (b)

    Every vertex in V⁡[u]∖Su,vV[u]\setminus S_{u,v} has a different neighborhood in X⁡[u]X[u] than the vertices in Su,vS_{u,v}.

Putting it together, in summary, we have shown the following.

Claim 7.11

In polynomial time we can uniquely identify all the subsets Su,v,v∈V′S_{u,v},v\in V^{\prime}, each of size p−1p-1, forming a partition of V⁡[u]V[u], for each u∈V12u\in V_{12}.

Thus, we have identified the subsets Su,v⊂V⁡[u]S_{u,v}\subset V[u] for v∈V′v\in V^{\prime}. We now need to label the elements of Su,vS_{u,v} by vectors {α​u¯+v¯∣α∈𝔽p∗}\{\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v}\mid\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{*}_{p}\}.

Claim 7.12

Assuming XX is a symplectic graph, for each v∈V′v\in V^{\prime} and u∈V12u\in V_{12}, we can label the p−1p-1 vertices in Su,vS_{u,v} by the p−1p-1 vectors α​u¯+v¯,α∈𝔽p∗\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v},\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{*}_{p} arbitrarily to get a labeling for V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} that is consistent with the labeling of V′V^{\prime}.

Proof of Claim. We first observe that adjacencies within V⁡[u]V[u] and between V⁡[u]V[u] and V′V^{\prime} are consistent with such a labeling by the arguments preceding the claim.

We now examine the adjacencies across two disjoint V⁡[u]V[u] and V⁡[u′]V[u^{\prime}]. Consider Su,v⊂V⁡[u]S_{u,v}\subset V[u] and Su′,v′⊂V⁡[u′]S_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}}\subset V[u^{\prime}]. There is an edge between these subsets if and only if for some non-zero scalars α\alpha and β\beta we have ⟨α​u¯+v¯,β​u′¯+v′¯⟩=0\langle\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v},\beta\bar{u^{\prime}}+\bar{v^{\prime}}\rangle=0. Now, ⟨u¯,u′¯⟩≠0\langle\bar{u},\bar{u^{\prime}}\rangle\neq 0. Hence we must have

α​β=−⟨v¯,v′¯⟩⟨u¯,u′¯⟩.\alpha\beta=\frac{-\langle\bar{v},\bar{v^{\prime}}\rangle}{\langle\bar{u},\bar{u^{\prime}}\rangle}.

Since α\alpha and β\beta are non-zero scalars, it follows that ⟨v¯,v′¯⟩≠0\langle\bar{v},\bar{v^{\prime}}\rangle\neq 0. It follows that vv and v′v^{\prime} being non-adjacent in the graph induced by V′V^{\prime} is a necessary condition for SvS_{v} and Sv′S_{v^{\prime}} to have any edges between them. Furthermore, the above equation implies that for the vertex, say vα∈Su,vv_{\alpha}\in S_{u,v} labeled α​u¯+v¯\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v} there is a unique β≠0\beta\neq 0 such that vαv_{\alpha} is adjacent to the vertex, say vβ′v^{\prime}_{\beta} in Su′,v′S_{u^{\prime},v^{\prime}} labeled β​u′¯+v′¯\beta\bar{u^{\prime}}+\bar{v^{\prime}}. Hence, either there are no edges between SvS_{v} and Sv′S_{v^{\prime}} (if vv and v′v^{\prime} are adjacent) or there is a perfect matching between SvS_{v} and Sv′S_{v^{\prime}}( if vv and v′v^{\prime} are non-adjacent).

Since these are all the possible edges in V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} and it is clearly consistent with any labeling of Su,vS_{u,v} by the p−1p-1 vectors α​u¯+v¯,α≠0\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v},\alpha\neq 0 for all u∈V12u\in V_{12} and v∈V′v\in V^{\prime}, this completes the proof of the claim.

Putting it together, clearly if XX is the symplectic graph of some non-degenerate symplectic form on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) the above algorithm verifies that by constructing a symplectic form consistent with the symplectic graph. The algorithm is described as a recursive procedure below. Essentially, given a graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) with |V|=p2​r|V|=p^{2r} vertices as input it will try to compute a labeling of VV by the p2​rp^{2r} vectors in V(2r,p)={∑i=1r(αix¯i+βiy¯i)∣αi,βi∈𝔽p}V(2r,p)=\{\sum_{i=1}^{r}(\alpha_{i}\bar{x}_{i}+\beta_{i}\bar{y}_{i})\mid\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\}, such that the edges of XX are consistent with some symplectic form on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p). If XX is a symplectic graph it will succeed. Otherwise, the procedure will fail and detect that XX is not symplectic.

Procedure Label(X,2​r,p)(X,2r,p)

  1. The procedure takes as input a simple graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) with p2​rp^{2r} vertices for an odd prime pp and computes a labeling consistent with some symplectic form on V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) if XX is a symplectic graph. Otherwise, it returns “fail”.

  2. (a)

    Identify the unique dominant vertex v0∈Vv_{0}\in V and label it by 00 (the zero vector).

  3. (b)

    Pick any pair of nonadjacent vertices x1,y1∈V∖{v0}x_{1},y_{1}\in V\setminus\{v_{0}\} and label them by the basis vectors x¯1\bar{x}_{1} and y¯1\bar{y}_{1} respectively.

  4. (c)

    Let V′V^{\prime} be the set of all vertices adjacent to both x1x_{1} and y1y_{1}. Check |V′|=p2​r−2|V^{\prime}|=p^{2r-2}. Let X′X^{\prime} be the subgraph induced by V′V^{\prime}. Recursively call Label(X′,2​r−2,p)(X^{\prime},2r-2,p) and obtain a labeling of V′V^{\prime} by vectors in V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) defined by the basis x¯i,y¯i,2≤i≤p\bar{x}_{i},\bar{y}_{i},2\leq i\leq p and consistent with a symplectic form on V⁡(2​r−2,p)V(2r-2,p) (Claim 7.7).

  5. (d)

    Determine the p2−1p^{2}-1 vertices V12V_{12} (Claim 7.8) consisting of vertices in V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} that are adjacent to all vertices in V′V^{\prime}. Determine the partition of V12V_{12} into p+1p+1 many (p−1)(p-1)-cliques in the induced subgraph G12G_{12} (Claim 7.9).

  6. (e)

    From the adjacencies between V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} and V′V^{\prime} determine the partition of V∖V′V\setminus V^{\prime} into p+1p+1 subsets V⁡[u]V[u] (Claim 7.10).

  7. (f)

    From the subgraphs G⁡[u]G[u] induced by the respective V⁡[u]V[u], determine the partition of V⁡[u]V[u] into p−1p-1-subsets Su,v,v∈V′S_{u,v},v\in V^{\prime} (Claim 7.11).

  8. (g)

    Label the vertices in Su,v,v∈V′S_{u,v},v\in V^{\prime} and u∈V12u\in V_{12} by the vectors α​u¯+v¯,α≠0\alpha\bar{u}+\bar{v},\alpha\neq 0 (Claim 7.12).

  9. (h)

    If any step above does not satisfy the stated property then output fail. Else output pass along with the complete labeling of VV by elements of V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) as the witness that XX is a symplectic graph.

Running time analysis  Let T⁡(n)T(n) denote the running time for constructing a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle for V⁡(2​r,p)V(2r,p) consistent with XX as the symplectic graph, where n=p2​rn=p^{2r} is the number of vertices in XX. The inductive construction and the rest of the computation implies the recurrence T⁡(n)=O⁡(|V|2)+T⁡(n−1)T(n)=O(|V|^{2})+T(n-1), which gives an overall cubic bound T⁡(n)=O⁡(|V|3)=O⁡(p6​r+3)T(n)=O(|V|^{3})=O(p^{6r+3}) on the running time.

Putting it together, we have a polynomial-time algorithm that checks if XX is the symplectic graph for the symplectic space by finding out a labeling of vertices by the vectors along with a consistent symplectic form. ∎

In summary, we have the following.

Theorem 7.13

Given a graph X=(V,E)X=(V,E) with p2​r+1p^{2r+1} vertices we can determine in polynomial time if it is the commuting graph of an extraspecial group of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1} and, if so, label vertices by unique group elements satisfying the commuting relation.

Proof 13

By Lemma 7.3 we can obtain the graph Xs=(Vs,Es)X_{s}=(V_{s},E_{s}) from XX in polynomial time. By Theorem 7.6 we can check if XsX_{s} is the symplectic graph of a symplectic form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle on V⁡(2​n,p)V(2n,p) and also find the symplectic form.

From the proof of Lemma 7.3, we have the following observations.

  • (a)

    The vertex of degree |Vs|−1|V_{s}|-1 in XsX_{s} is the 00 element of V⁡(2​n,p)V(2n,p), and corresponds to ZZ in GG.

  • (b)

    For each vertex x∈Vsx\in V_{s} there is a closed-twins equivalence class of size p−1p-1 containing xx. There is a corresponding subset of vertices Hx∖ZH_{x}\setminus Z in XX of size p2−pp^{2}-p, where HxH_{x}, in turn, corresponds to a subgroup of GG of order p2p^{2} that contains ZZ. We have a labeling of the vertex xx by a linear combination ∑i=1n(αi​x¯i+βi​y¯i)\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\alpha_{i}\bar{x}_{i}+\beta_{i}\bar{y}_{i}), and the remaining p−2p-2 vertices in the equivalence class are labeled by non-zero scalar multiples of this linear combination.

Now, using the description of the extraspecial group G1G_{1} we can label the vertices of the clique Hx∖ZH_{x}\setminus Z with the group elements

zj⋅(∏i=1nxiαi.yiβi)k,0≤j≤p−1,1≤k≤p−1.z^{j}\cdot\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}.y_{i}^{\beta_{i}}\right)^{k},0\leq j\leq p-1,1\leq k\leq p-1.

This will give us the labeling of XX with the elements of the extraspecial group G1G_{1} of order p2​r+1p^{2r+1}, consistent with the commuting graph XX.

Observe that if XsX_{s} is not a symplectic graph then Procedure Label described in Theorem 7.6 will detect that and return fail. This completes the proof. ∎

8 A quasipolynomial time algorithm in the general case

Assuming CFSG (the Classification of Finite Simple Groups [42]), in this section we present a 2O⁡(log3⁡n)2^{O(\log^{3}n)} time algorithm for checking if a given nn-vertex graph is the commuting graph of some nn-element group and, if so, labeling the vertices of the graph by the group elements consistent with all the commuting pairs. For CFSG in this section we will refer to the (concrete) constructions of finite simple groups described in Wilson’s text [83].

  1. (a)

    Our main idea is the notion of description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for any finite group GG that we develop in this section. It is essentially an encoding of the group GG as a binary string of length at most c⋅log3⁡|G|c\cdot\log^{3}|G|, for some fixed constant c>0c>0, from which GG can be recovered efficiently. More precisely, we will describe an algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} that takes as input a binary string ww and, if w=desc(G)w=\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for some finite group GG the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} will computes the multiplication table of GG as output in time polynomial in |G||G|. Otherwise, the algorithm will reject ww as an invalid description.

  2. (b)

    We note that this algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} can be used to generate the multiplication tables of all groups GG of order nn as follows. We enumerate all possible binary strings ww of length at most c⋅log3⁡nc\cdot\log^{3}n. For each such ww we run the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} on it. If w=desc(G)w=\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for some GG then 𝒟\mathcal{D} will output its multiplication table. We compute Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) from GG and check if XX is isomorphic to Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) in time 2O⁡(log3⁡n)2^{O(\log^{3}n)} using Babai’s graph isomorphism algorithm [4].

Thus, the main task of this section is to define desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) and describe the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D}. We will first define desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for finite simple groups, along with how the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} will compute the multiplication table for GG given desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) as input. We will then extend the notion of desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) to all groups by using a composition series for GG combined with desc(N)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(N) for each composition factor NN of GG.

Remark 5

We emphasize here that our notion of “short” description is entirely different from the well-studied notion of generator-relator presentations of groups (see e.g. [5]). Indeed, desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) and its construction will be significantly simpler. It suffices for the purpose of recovering the multiplication table of the group GG in time polynomial in |G||G|.

8.1 Short descriptions for finite simple groups assuming CFSG

We first briefly summarize the classification theorem of finite simple groups (CFSG) [42]. A finite simple group is one of the following:

  • (a)

    A cyclic group of prime order.

  • (b)

    An alternating group An,n≥5A_{n},n\geq 5.

  • (c)

    A finite simple group of Lie type.

  • (d)

    A sporadic finite simple group.

As there are only finite many sporadic finite simple groups, for the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} they can be trivially dealt with. The cyclic groups of prime order are also easy to deal with for the algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} as there is a unique such subgroup of order pp for each prime pp.

Lemma 8.1

If GG is cyclic of prime order pp then desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) can be defined as the binary encoding bin(p)\mathop{\mathrm{bin}}(p) of pp which is of length log⁡p\log p bits. We can include 11 as the generator with the additive group ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} as the group it encodes.

Proof 14

The algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} will take the binary encoding bin(p)\mathop{\mathrm{bin}}(p) of pp, verify that pp is prime using the polynomial-time primality test, and then write out the group table for the additive group of integers modulo pp. ∎

For several of the remaining cases, the following simple lemma gives a framework for defining desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) and computing GG’s multiplication table from it. We use the well-known fact that any finite simple group can be generated with two elements (see [59]).

Lemma 8.2

Let HH be a finite group and N⊲K≤HN\lhd K\leq H be subgroups such that

  • (a)

    desc(H)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(H) is of length mm.

  • (b)

    The multiplication table for HH can be computed from desc(H)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(H) in time polynomial in |H||H|.

  • (c)

    We can test membership of elements in NN in time polynomial in |H||H|.

Suppose G=K/NG=K/N is simple. Then desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) has size O⁡(m+log⁡|H|)O(m+\log|H|) and in time polynomial in |H||H| we can compute the multiplication table for GG.

Proof 15

As G=K/NG=K/N is simple it can be generated by two elements N​g1,N​g2∈K/NNg_{1},Ng_{2}\in K/N where g1,g2∈Kg_{1},g_{2}\in K. Let desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) be the indices of these two elements in HH along with desc(H)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(H). By indices here we mean the positions of these elements in the multiplication table for HH. The two indices into HH are of size O⁡(log⁡|H|)O(\log|H|). Therefore, desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) is of size O⁡(m+log⁡|H|)O(m+\log|H|). The claimed algorithm 𝒟\mathcal{D} will first use desc(H)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(H) to compute the multiplication table for HH. It can enumerate HH and use the indices to identify the elements g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} in HH. Using the multiplication table for HH it can generate the subgroup K=⟨g1,g2⟩K=\langle g_{1},g_{2}\rangle, listing down all its elements in time polynomial in |H||H|. Next, the algorithm can identify the normal subgroup NN (as given in the hypothesis) in time polynomial in |H||H| and obtain the multiplication table for G=K/NG=K/N.∎

We will apply the above lemma to the remaining cases of finite simple groups.

Lemma 8.3

If G=AnG=A_{n} for some n≥5n\geq 5 then we can define desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) of size O⁡(log⁡|G|)O(\log|G|).

Proof 16

We can define desc(An)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(A_{n}) as the encoding of two generators of AnA_{n}, by giving the index of the two generating permutations, say g1,g2g_{1},g_{2} in SnS_{n}, where we consider the lexicographic order of enumeration of SnS_{n}. More precisely, each element π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} as an nn-tuple (1π,2π,…,nπ)(1^{\pi},2^{\pi},\ldots,n^{\pi}) and the enumeration begins with (1,2,…,n)(1,2,\ldots,n) and ends with (n,n−1,…,1)(n,n-1,\ldots,1). Hence, desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) will be of size 2​log⁡n!=O⁡(log⁡|An|)2\log n!=O(\log|A_{n}|). We can now apply Lemma 8.2 with H=SnH=S_{n}, K=AnK=A_{n} and N={1}N=\{1\} to complete the proof.∎

We now consider the finite simple groups of Lie type. It is convenient to deal with them in two categories: classical and exceptional. We will follow the (concrete) constructions of these groups as explained in Wilson’s text [83].

8.1.1 Classical Lie type

We begin by describing a useful algorithm for efficiently enumerating elements of the finite matrix group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q).

Lemma 8.4

There is an algorithm that takes as input the pair (n,q)(n,q) encoded in binary, where qq is a prime power, and enumerates all elements of the group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) of n×nn\times n invertible matrices over the field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} in time polynomial in |GLn(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|.

Proof 17

We first recall construction of the finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} given qq in binary representation. The text [55, Chapter 25.4] contains more details. Let q=pkq=p^{k} for a prime pp. Then 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is a degree-kk extension of the prime field 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. The elements of 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} are essentially the residues {0,1,…,p−1}\{0,1,\ldots,p-1\} modulo the prime pp, each of which can be represented in binary with at most log⁡p\log p bits. Field arithmetic in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is addition and multiplication modulo pp. These operations can be performed using O⁡((log⁡p)2)O((\log p)^{2}) bit operations. The finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is described by a monic irreducible polynomial g​(y)∈𝔽p​[y]g(y)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}[y] of degree kk. Such a polynomial g⁡(y)g(y) can be found by looking through all the pk=qp^{k}=q many monic degree-kk polynomials in 𝔽p​[y]\mathbb{F}_{p}[y] and testing each for irreducibility until we find one. This algorithm is correct as irreducible polynomials are guaranteed to exist, and it has polynomial in log⁡q\log q running time (see [55, Chapter 12] for details). Now, the elements of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} can be represented as degree at most k−1k-1 polynomials over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} (the residues of polynomials in 𝔽p​[y]\mathbb{F}_{p}[y] modulo g⁡(y)g(y)). Clearly, the size of g⁡(y)=∑i=0kαi​xig(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_{i}x^{i} in binary is O⁡(k​log⁡p)=O⁡(log⁡q)O(k\log p)=O(\log q) and arithmetic operations in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is essentially addition and multiplication of degree k−1k-1 polynomials in 𝔽p​[y]\mathbb{F}_{p}[y] modulo g⁡(y)g(y). Each such operation can be performed in O⁡((log⁡q)3)O((\log q)^{3}) time.

The elements of the group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) consists of n×nn\times n invertible matrices over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. Each such matrix can be identified with the nn-tuple of its linearly independent column vectors (v1,v2,…,vn)(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{n}) in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The order of the group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) is given by

|GLn(q)|=(qn−1)⋅(qn−q)⋯(qn−qi)⋯(qn−qn−1),|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|=(q^{n}-1)\cdot(q^{n}-q)\cdots(q^{n}-q^{i})\cdots(q^{n}-q^{n-1}),

where the (i+1)s​t(i+1)^{st} term qn−qiq^{n}-q^{i} in the product, i≤n−1i\leq n-1, is the number of choices for the vector vi+1v_{i+1} such that it is independent of {v1,…,vi}\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}\}. Hence, the set LiL_{i} of all ii-tuples (v1,v2,…,vi)(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i}) of linearly independent vectors in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is of cardinality |Li|=∏j=0i(qn−qj)|L_{i}|=\prod_{j=0}^{i}(q^{n}-q^{j}), which is upper bounded by |GLn(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|. The enumeration algorithm takes as input the pair (n,q)(n,q) encoded in binary (which is of size O⁡(log⁡n+log⁡q)O(\log n+\log q)). It will compute the sets LiL_{i} for increasing values of i,1≤i≤ni,1\leq i\leq n, until finally the set LnL_{n} yields a listing of all elements of GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q). To begin with, L1L_{1} consists of all the qn−1q^{n}-1 many nonzero vectors in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. Suppose now, in the it​hi^{th} stage, the algorithm has computed the list LiL_{i}. To compute Li+1L_{i+1} the algorithm will cycle through all tuples (v1,v2,…,vi)∈Li(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i})\in L_{i}. For each such tuple it will examine all nonzero vectors v∈𝔽qnv\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} one by one performing a linear independence test. If the vector v∈𝔽qnv\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} is linearly independent of (v1,v2,…,vi)(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i}) the algorithm includes the (i+1)(i+1)-tuple (v1,v2,…,vi,v)(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i},v) in Li+1L_{i+1}. At the end of this stage the algorithm would have computed the set Li+1L_{i+1}. The time taken for this stage is clearly bounded by |Li|⋅qn|L_{i}|\cdot q^{n} many linear independence tests, that is, checking if vv is independent of {v1,v2,…,vi}\{v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{i}\}. Using Gaussian elimination [68, Section 3.3] independence test can be done with O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) many field arithmetic operations.

To complete the running time analysis notice that, as q≥2q\geq 2 and n≥1n\geq 1, |GLn(q)|≥qn/2|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|\geq q^{n}/2. Thus, the total number of field arithmetic operations required over all nn stages is bounded by O⁡(n⋅|GLn(q)|⋅qn)=O⁡(n​|GLn(q)|2)O(n\cdot|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|\cdot q^{n})=O(n|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|^{2}). As already noted, each field operation in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} can be performed with O⁡((log⁡q)3)O((\log q)^{3}) many bit operations. This completes the proof.

Lemma 8.5

For each finite simple group GG that is of classical Lie type, there is a description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) of O⁡(log⁡|G|)O(\log|G|) size such that the multiplication table for GG can be computed from desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) in time polynomial in |G||G|.

Proof 18

These finite simple groups are categorized below, following Wilson’s text [83, Chapter 3].

  1. (a)

    PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) for either n>2n>2 or q>3q>3. These are the projective special linear group arising from the matrix group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) (the finite group of n×nn\times n invertible matrices over the finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}).

  2. (b)

    PSp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) which is the projective symplectic group, obtained as quotient of the symplectic group Sp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q), and where Sp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) itself is a subgroup of GL2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{2m}(q).

  3. (c)

    PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) which is the projective unitary group, obtained as a quotient of the special unitary group SUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{n}(q). The general unitary group GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) itself is a subgroup of the matrix group GLn(q2)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q^{2}).

  4. (d)

    Finally, the orthogonal groups which are also obtained essentially as quotients of matrix groups, but there are different subcases depending on both nn and qq.

Consider PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q). The special linear group

SLn(q)={A∈GLn(q)∣det(A)=1}\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)=\{A\in\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)\mid\det(A)=1\}

is a subgroup of GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) of index q−1q-1. PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) is obtained as the quotient SLn(q)/Z\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)/Z where ZZ consists of all “scalar matrices” λ​In\lambda I_{n} of determinant 11. Thus, |PSLn(q)|≥|GLn(q)|/q2|\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|\geq|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|/q^{2}. We can apply Lemma 8.2, letting H=GLn(q)H=\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q), K=SLn(q)K=\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) and N=ZN=Z in it. By Lemma 8.4, the group GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) has a description of size O⁡(log⁡n+log⁡q)O(\log n+\log q). With that description the algorithm of Lemma 8.4 is an algorithm will enumerate all elements of GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) in time polynomial in |GLn(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|. Now, applying Lemma 8.2 we can obtain the desired description for PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q).

Next, consider PSp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q). Recall that the symplectic group Sp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) is the subgroup of GL2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) consisting of all isometries of a non-singular alternating bilinear form on the vector space 𝔽q2​m\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2m}. It turns out that |Sp2​m(q)|>qm2|\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q)|>q^{m^{2}}. As |GL2​m(q)|=q4​m2|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{2m}(q)|=q^{4m^{2}}, clearly

|GL2​m(q)|≤|Sp2​m(q)|4.|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{2m}(q)|\leq|\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q)|^{4}.

Thus, the description of the group Sp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) is easy to construct. Given 2​m2m and qq in binary, in time polynomial in mm and qq we can define a non-singular alternating bilinear form ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle on 𝔽q2​m\mathbb{F}_{q}^{2m}. Then, as done for the previous case, we can enumerate the elements of GL2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{2m}(q), one by one, and put each into Sp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) if it is an isometry for ⟨,⟩\langle,\rangle. Now, the simple group PSp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) by quotienting out the subgroup of scalar matrices (which has size at most 22). Clearly, Lemma 8.2 can be applied to obtain the desired description for PSp2​m(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{2m}(q) along with the algorithm for obtaining its multiplication table.

For the next case PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q), we start with the group GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) which is the subgroup of GLn(q2)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q^{2}) that preserves the sesquilinear form ⟨x,y⟩=∑i=1nxi​yiq\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}^{q}. From there on the process of obtaining SUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) and then PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) is exactly like in the case of PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q). In order to obtain the desired description for PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) it suffices to generate GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) in time polynomial in |PSUn(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q)| given nn and qq. Clearly, the entire group GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) can be listed down in time polynomial in |GLn(q2)||\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q^{2})| by enumerating, one by one, each n×nn\times n invertible matrix MM over 𝔽q2\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}} and checking if MM is in GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) (by checking if it preserves the sesquilinear form ⟨x,y⟩\langle x,y\rangle defined above). However, |GLn(q2)|<|GUn(q)|3|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q^{2})|<|\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q)|^{3}. Thus, the brute-force algorithm for generating all of GLn(q2)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q^{2}) by looking through all n×nn\times n invertible matrices over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and picking those which preserve the sesquilinear form will again work. Finally, the group PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) is only smaller than GUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) by a small power of qq.

The fourth category are the simple groups arising from the orthogonal groups. There are different cases to consider here.

When qq is odd, there are exactly two non-singular nn-variate symmetric bilinear forms over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. If ff is one of them then GOn(f)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits_{n}(f) is the subgroup of GLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) that leaves ff invariant. If n=2​m+1n=2m+1 is odd, it turns out that there is only one orthogonal group which we may denote by GO2​m+1(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q). We can then construct SO2​m+1(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SO}}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q) and PSO2​m+1(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSO}}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q) analogous to the earlier cases. But there is a further subgroup of index 22 in PSO2​m+1(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSO}}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q) denoted P​Ω2​m+1⁡(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q). As before, we can apply Lemma 8.2 to obtain the desired description of P​Ω2​m+1⁡(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits_{2m+1}(q) from which the group’s multiplication table can be obtained in polynomial time.

For n=2​mn=2m, there are two orthogonal groups GO2​m+(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits^{+}_{2m}(q) and GO2​m−(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits^{-}_{2m}(q). As in the previous case we can obtain the groups P​Ω2​mϵ⁡(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{\epsilon}_{2m}(q) for ϵ∈{+,−1}\epsilon\in\{+,-1\}. For odd qq these are always simple and Lemma 8.2 is again easily applicable.

The characteristic 22 case of orthogonal groups requires different techniques. However, Lemma 8.2 is still applicable in defining desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for the simple groups GG arising in this case. We omit the details.∎

8.1.2 Exceptional Lie type

We will closely follow Wilson’s exposition [83, Chapter 4]. These finite simple groups come in ten families:

  • (a)

    The five families of Chevalley groups G2​(q)G_{2}(q), F4​(q)F_{4}(q), and En​(q),n∈{6,7,8}E_{n}(q),n\in\{6,7,8\}.

  • (b)

    The two families of Steinberg–Tits–Herzig groups D43​(q){}^{3}{D}_{4}(q) and E62​(q){}^{2}{E}_{6}(q).

  • (c)

    The Suzuki and Ree groups Sz(22​n+1)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(2^{2n+1}), R1​(32​n+1)R_{1}(3^{2n+1}) and R2​(22​n+1)R_{2}(2^{2n+1}) (also known as B22​(q){}^{2}B_{2}(q), G22​(q){}^{2}G_{2}(q) and F42​(q){}^{2}F_{4}(q) for the appropriate qq).

Unlike the classical case, these families have only one parameter which is the field size qq. It turns out that the following lemma (analogous to Lemma 8.2) captures how these simple groups arise and suggest a suitable desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for each GG along with the corresponding algorithm for recovering GG from desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G).

Lemma 8.6

Let GG be finite simple group from any of the ten families listed above. Then we can define a description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) of size O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q) such that GG’s multiplication table can be obtained from it in time polynomial in |G||G|.

Proof 19

We will briefly describe how the groups are constructed for each of these ten families. The easy descriptions and algorithms for generating their multiplication tables will suggest themselves.

  1. (a)

    Sz(22​n+1)=B22​(22​n+1)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(2^{2n+1})={}^{2}B_{2}(2^{2n+1}):   Let q=22​n+1q=2^{2n+1}. The Suzuki group Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) (see [83, Chapter 4.2]) can be considered as a subgroup of the group GL4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{4}(q). As Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) is simple, it can be generated with just two generators [59]. Since |GL4(q)|≤q16|\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{4}(q)|\leq q^{16}, we can describe these generators g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} as two indices i1i_{1} and i2i_{2}, respectively, each of size 16​log⁡q16\log q bits. Define desc(Sz(q))\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)) as the triple (i1,i2,q)(i_{1},i_{2},q) which is of O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q) size with the indices and qq encoded in binary. The algorithm for recovering the multiplication table of Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) in time polynomial in |Sz(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)| is as follows: it first enumerates the elements of GL4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{4}(q). The elements M1,M2∈GL4(q)M_{1},M_{2}\in\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{4}(q) at the i1t​hi_{1}^{th} and i2t​hi_{2}^{th} positions in the enumeration generate Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q). Starting with M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} we generate all elements of Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) in at most |Sz(q)||\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)| rounds. Let S0={M1,M2}S_{0}=\{M_{1},M_{2}\}. Inductively, suppose after jj rounds we have computed Sj⊆Sz(q)S_{j}\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q). Set Sj+1={M⋅Mi∣i∈{1,2}​ and ​M∈Sj}S_{j+1}=\{M\cdot M_{i}\mid i\in\{1,2\}\textrm{ and }M\in S_{j}\}. If Sj+1=SjS_{j+1}=S_{j} the algorithm outputs SjS_{j} and stops. As ⟨M1,M2⟩=Sz(q)\langle M_{1},M_{2}\rangle=\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) the output SjS_{j} is Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q). This algorithm actually enumerates Sz(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q) as a subset of GL4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{4}(q) in time polynomial in qq, and its multiplication table can be easily computed from this enumeration.

  2. (b)

    G2​(q)G_{2}(q):  It turns out that G2​(q)G_{2}(q) (see [83, Chapter 4.3]) arises as the automorphism group of the octonion algebra over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The entire octonion algebra can be listed in time O⁡(q8)O(q^{8}). As the automorphisms fix the identity in the octonion algebra, G2​(q)G_{2}(q) is essentially a subgroup of GO7(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits_{7}(q). We can enumerate GO7(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GO}}\nolimits_{7}(q) and pick out the automorphisms which will give us G2​(q)G_{2}(q). As |G2​(q)||G_{2}(q)| is q6​(q6−1)​(q2−1)q^{6}(q^{6}-1)(q^{2}-1), this will be polynomial time in the group size. We can define the desc(G2​(q))\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G_{2}(q)) of size O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q). It is essentially just the encoding of qq.

  3. (c)

    R1​(32​n+1)=G22​(32​n+1)R_{1}(3^{2n+1})={}^{2}G_{2}(3^{2n+1}): This can be handled quite analogously to G2​(q)G_{2}(q) [83, Section 4.5].

  4. (d)

    D43​(q){}^{3}{D}_{4}(q):  This group (see [83, Chapter 4.6]) arises as centralizer of a certain order 33 automorphism of P​Ω8+⁡(q3)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{+}_{8}(q^{3}). Because of the special nature of this automorphism (a product of a field automorphism and the triality automorphism), it has a short description of size O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q). As P​Ω8+⁡(q3)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{+}_{8}(q^{3}) can be enumerated in time polynomial in qq, we can pick out the centralizer elements in time polynomial in qq.

  5. (e)

    F4​(q)F_{4}(q):  when qq is not a power of 22 or 33, F4​(q)F_{4}(q) arises as automorphisms of the finite (non-associative) Albert algebra which is 2727-dimensional [83, Chapter 4.8]. Thus, F4​(q)F_{4}(q) can be picked out from GL27(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{27}(q) by enumerating it and checking each element for being an automorphism. The finite Albert algebra can be defined in O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q) size by defining the multiplication of its basis elements.

  6. (f)

    R2​(22​n+1)=F42​(22​n+1)R_{2}(2^{2n+1})={}^{2}F_{4}(2^{2n+1}):  This case is quite similar to the previous one [83, Section 4.9].

  7. (g)

    E6​(q)E_{6}(q):  This group can be defined as automorphisms of a certain trilinear form over the Albert algebra [83, Chapter 4.10]. After quotienting out the scalar subgroup from this automorphism group we will obtain E6​(q)E_{6}(q). The same algorithm of enumerating the bigger group and selecting the automorphisms and then quotienting out the scalars will work.

  8. (h)

    E7​(q)E_{7}(q) and E8​(q)E_{8}(q):  Both these arise as automorphisms of a finite Lie algebra [83, Chapter 4.1 non-zero vector u¯∈Span(x¯1,y¯1)\bar{u}\in\mathop{\mathrm{Span}}(\bar{x}_{1},\bar{y}_{1}). 2]. For E8​(q)E_{8}(q) we have to consider a 248248-dimensional Lie algebra. Thus we can look for E8​(q)E_{8}(q) inside GL248(q)\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}\nolimits_{248}(q) by enumerating all its elements and picking out the automorphisms. All we need is that from a O⁡(log⁡q)O(\log q) size description we should be able to obtain the Lie algebra. For that we only need to express the multiplication of basis elements as an 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} linear combination of the basis (which is of size 248248). E7​(q)E_{7}(q) is similarly dealt with as automorphisms of a smaller dimensional Lie algebra.∎

The above lemmas immediately imply the following.

Theorem 8.7

There is an algorithm that, given as input desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for a finite simple group GG, outputs its multiplication table in time polynomial in |G||G|.

8.2 Short descriptions for finite groups

We first show that every finite group GG has a description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) of bit-length O⁡((log⁡|G|)3)O((\log|G|)^{3}). Then we describe the algorithm that given as input a bit string yy, if y=desc(G)y=\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for some finite group GG then the algorithm runs in time 2O⁡((log⁡|G|)3)2^{O((\log|G|)^{3})} and outputs the multiplication table of a group G′G^{\prime} isomorphic to GG.

Building on the construction of desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for finite simple groups GG, described in Section 8.1, we obtain desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for all finite groups with a straightforward construction that uses a composition series for GG. It is convenient to use Erdős-Rényi cube generating sequences [34].

Definition 5 (Erdős-Rényi cube generating sequences)

Let GG be a finite group. A cube generating sequence (abbreviated as c.g.s.) for GG is a sequence (g1,g2,…,gk)(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{k}) of elements from GG such that

G={g1ϵ1g2ϵ2⋯gkϵk∣ϵi∈{0,1} for each i}.G=\{g_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}}g_{2}^{\epsilon_{2}}\cdots g_{k}^{\epsilon_{k}}\mid\epsilon_{i}\in\{0,1\}\hbox{ for each }i\}.

Thus, given the cube generating sequence (g1,g2,…,gk)(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{k}), each element of GG can be defined by the bit vector (ϵ1,ϵ2,…,ϵk)(\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2},\ldots,\epsilon_{k}). We note that this bit vector need not be unique for a group element.

Theorem 8.8

[34] Every finite group GG has a cube generating sequence of size at most 2​log⁡|G|2\log|G|.

Let X=(g1,g2,…,gk)X=(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{k}) be cube generating sequence for a group GG. Its length kk is denoted |X||X|. Abusing notation, by g∈Xg\in X we will mean that g=gig=g_{i} for some ii.

We note that cube generating sequences can be computed in polynomial time.

Lemma 8.9

There is a polynomial-time algorithm that takes a group GG by its multiplication table as input and outputs a cube-generating sequence of length at most 2​log⁡|G|2\log|G| for GG.

Proof 20

The simple algorithm is directly based on a “cube doubling” trick due to Babai and Szemerédi [6]. Suppose we have picked the sequence (g1,g2,…,gi)(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{i}) of group elements from GG. Let CiC_{i} be the cube it generates. That is,

Ci={g1ϵ1g2ϵ2⋯giϵi∣ϵj∈{0,1} for 1≤j≤i}.C_{i}=\{g_{1}^{\epsilon_{1}}g_{2}^{\epsilon_{2}}\cdots g_{i}^{\epsilon_{i}}\mid\epsilon_{j}\in\{0,1\}\hbox{ for }1\leq j\leq i\}.

For any g∈Gg\in G let Ci​g={x​g∣x∈Ci}C_{i}g=\{xg\mid x\in C_{i}\}. As |Ci|≤2i|C_{i}|\leq 2^{i} and each element in CiC_{i} can be computed with i−1i-1 group multiplications, the set CiC_{i} can be enumerated with at most (i−1)​2i(i-1)2^{i} many group multiplications. We can enumerate Ci​gC_{i}g with 2i2^{i} additional group multiplications.

Now, if Ci​g∩Ci≠∅C_{i}g\cap C_{i}\neq\emptyset for g∈Gg\in G then gg is in the cube generated by the sequence (gi−1,gi−1−1,…,g1−1,g1,…,gi)(g_{i}^{-1},g_{i-1}^{-1},\ldots,g_{1}^{-1},g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}). Thus, if for all g∈Gg\in G we have Ci​g∩Ci≠∅C_{i}g\cap C_{i}\neq\emptyset then we have a cube generating sequence of length 2​i2i. Otherwise, there is a gi+1∈Gg_{i+1}\in G such that

Ci​gi+1∩Ci=∅,C_{i}g_{i+1}\cap C_{i}=\emptyset,

and the cube Ci+1C_{i+1} generated by (g1,g2,…,gi+1)(g_{1},g_{2},\ldots,g_{i+1}) is twice the cardinality of CiC_{i} by a simple counting argument. Clearly, we can find gi+1g_{i+1} in time polynomial in |G||G| by searching through GG.

As |Ci+1|=2⋅|Ci||C_{i+1}|=2\cdot|C_{i}|, it follows that this procedure will eventually find a cube generating sequence CkC_{k} for some k≤2​log⁡|G|k\leq 2\log|G| with at most polynomial in |G||G| group multiplications and hence in time polynomial in |G||G|. ∎

We now explain the construction of desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) for a finite group GG, where GG is given by its multiplication table. Compute a composition series for GG (which can be done in time polynomial in |G||G| by computing normal closures of elements):

1=N0⊲N1⊲⋯⊲Nr=G.1=N_{0}\lhd N_{1}\lhd\cdots\lhd N_{r}=G.

The above discussion has the following immediate consequence.

Lemma 8.11

Given as input the multiplication table of a finite group GG, there is an algorithm that computes in time polynomial in |G||G| its description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G).

However, we are interested in the converse statement, about generating GG from its description desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G) in time polynomial in |G||G|. The next theorem, which shows this, will allow us to enumerate the multiplication tables of all groups of order nn up to isomorphism in time 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})}.

Theorem 8.12

There is an algorithm that given as input desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G), for a finite group GG, outputs its multiplication table in time polynomial in |G||G|. As a consequence, there is an algorithm that outputs the list of multiplication tables of all distinct groups of order nn in time 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})}.
