The algorithm for enumerating all order nn group multiplication tables is easy to obtain from the above. We run through all strings ww of length at most c​log3​nc\log^{3}n, where n=|G|n=|G|, and apply the above algorithm to generate the multiplication for GG if ww encodes desc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{desc}}(G).

Notice that this enumeration may contain duplicates because the same group can have different composition series and hence different descriptions. We can eliminate the duplicates by running Miller’s group isomorphism test [61]. Each such test takes nlog⁡nn^{\log n}. Since there are at most 2log3⁡n2^{\log^{3}n} groups being listed the running time to detect multiplicities takes time at most 2log3⁡n⋅nlog⁡n⋅2log3⁡n=2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{\log^{3}n}\cdot n^{\log n}\cdot 2^{\log^{3}n}=2^{O((\log n)^{3})}.∎

Remark 6

Some notes concerning the preceding results:

  1. (a)

    Computing a composition series for GG can be done in time polynomial in |G||G| by computing normal closures of elements:

    1=N0⊳N1⊳⋯⊳Nr=G.1=N_{0}\rhd N_{1}\rhd\cdots\rhd N_{r}=G.

    More precisely, for each g∈Gg\in G we compute its normal closure by starting with the cyclic subgroup N=⟨g⟩N=\langle g\rangle and repeatedly replacing it with the (larger) subgroup generated by the set {xyx−1∣x∈G,y∈N}\{xyx^{-1}\mid x\in G,y\in N\} until NN does not grow any further. By construction, the final NN is a normal subgroup of GG and its computation takes time polynomial in |G||G|. If GG is not simple, then for some g∈Gg\in G this construction will yield a non-trivial normal subgroup NN. We can now recursively find composition series for NN and G/NG/N (we have multiplication tables for both) and put them together to obtain a composition series for GG in time polynomial in |G||G|.

  2. (b)

    For each group NiN_{i} we compute a cube generating sequence XiX_{i} of size at most ki≤2​log⁡|Ni|k_{i}\leq 2\log|N_{i}|. This computation is done in time polynomial in |Ni||N_{i}|, by Lemma 8.9. As part of the description of GG, for each 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r we obtain a set of relations RiR_{i} as defined in Equation (8).

Our algorithm described in Theorem 8.12 is broadly based on a result of McIver and Neumann [60] that bounds the number of nn element groups by 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})}. There is related work by Babai et al. [5] which shows that all simple groups of nn elements (except one family called the Ree groups) have generator-relator presentations of size O⁡((log⁡n)2)O((\log n)^{2}).

Theorem 8.14

There is a 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})} time algorithm that recognizes if a given nn-vertex graph is the commuting graph of a group of order nn.

Proof 23

Let XX be an nn-vertex graph. The algorithm cycles through all multiplication tables of distinct groups of order nn, listed by the 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})} time algorithm described in Theorem 8.12. For each group GG that is listed we can compute its commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) in polynomial time. We can test if Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is isomorphic to the input graph XX using Babai’s 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})} time algorithm [4].

Thus, the overall computation takes 2O⁡((log⁡n)3)2^{O((\log n)^{3})} time.∎

The algorithm of Theorem 8.14 does not reveal any new relationship between the group and its commuting graph. It would be more interesting to obtain an algorithm that exploits the commuting graph structure.

9 Isoclinism of groups and commuting graphs

Motivated by the polynomial-time algorithm for recognizing commuting graphs of extraspecial groups, in this section we briefly discuss isoclinism of groups and its connection to commuting graphs.

The lexicographic product of graphs Γ1\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\Gamma_{2} is the graph on the vertex set V⁡(Γ1)×V⁡(Γ2)V(\Gamma_{1})\times V(\Gamma_{2}), in which (v1,w1)(v_{1},w_{1}) and (v2,w2)(v_{2},w_{2}) are joined if and only if either v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are joined in Γ1\Gamma_{1}, or v1=v2v_{1}=v_{2} and w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} are joined in Γ2\Gamma_{2}. If Γ2\Gamma_{2} is a complete graph, then the lexicographic product is obtained from Γ1\Gamma_{1} by blowing up each vertex to a complete graph on |V​Γ2||V\Gamma_{2}| vertices.

Commutation in a group GG is a map from G×GG\times G to the derived group G′G^{\prime}; multiplying the arguments by elements of Z⁡(G)Z(G) does not change the function value, so commutation induces a map from G/Z⁡(G)×G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G)\times G/Z(G) to G′G^{\prime}. We say that groups GG and HH are isoclinic if there are isomorphisms θ:G/Z⁡(G)→H/Z⁡(H)\theta:G/Z(G)\to H/Z(H) and ϕ:G′→H′\phi:G^{\prime}\to H^{\prime} which intertwine the commutation map; that is, for all g1,g2∈Gg_{1},g_{2}\in G,

[θ⁡(g1​Z​(G)),θ⁡(g2​Z​(G))]=ϕ⁡([g1​Z​(G),g2​Z​(G)]).[\theta(g_{1}Z(G)),\theta(g_{2}Z(G))]=\phi([g_{1}Z(G),g_{2}Z(G)]).

Now the commuting graph of a group GG is the lexicographic product of a graph on G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G) with g1​Z​(G)g_{1}Z(G) and g2​Z​(G)g_{2}Z(G) joined if [g1,g2]=1[g_{1},g_{2}]=1 (this graph can also be described as the induced subgraph of the commuting graph of GG on a transversal for Z⁡(G)Z(G) in GG) with a complete graph on Z⁡(G)Z(G); the graph on G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G) is determined by the isoclinism type. Hence, as observed by Pezzott and Nakaoka [64], we have:

Theorem 9.1

Isoclinic groups of the same order have isomorphic commuting graphs.

Remark 7

It follows from Lemma 7.2 that the extraspecial groups G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, defined in Section 7, are isoclinic. Indeed, the recognition algorithm of Section 7 implicitly uses this property.

Is there a converse to Theorem 9.1? That is, if two groups have isomorphic commuting graphs, must they be isoclinic? This holds for various classes of groups, such as abelian groups, non-abelian simple groups, and extraspecial groups (as we have seen).

However, it is not true in general; we recycle an example taken from [24] to show this. Let GG be the group of order 6464 which is SmallGroup(64,182) in the SmallGroups library [10] in GAP [38]. A Schur cover of GG is a group HH of maximal order subject to having a subgroup Z≤H′∩Z⁡(H)Z\leq H^{\prime}\cap Z(H) such that H/Z≅GH/Z\cong G. The Schur multiplier of GG has order 22, so any Schur cover of GG has order 128128. Moreover, the Bogomolov multiplier (see [24] for context and other references) of GG is equal to the Schur multiplier, which implies that any Schur cover HH is commutation-preserving: that is, two elements a,b∈Ha,b\in H commute if and only if their projections Z​a,Z​b∈GZa,Zb\in G commute. This implies that the commuting graph of a Schur cover is obtained from the commuting graph of GG by replacing each vertex with a clique of size 22, with all edges between cliques corresponding to adjacent vertices. This procedure also describes the commuting graph of G×C2G\times C_{2}. On the other hand, it is easy to verify computationally that the derived groups of HH and G×C2G\times C_{2} are not isomorphic, so these groups cannot be isoclinic.

We note that the group GG has nilpotency class 33, as do all of its Schur covers (these are SmallGroup(128,ii) for i∈{789,790,791,815,816,817}i\in\{789,790,791,815,816,817\} in the GAP library). This suggested that it might be true that groups with nilpotency class 22 and isomorphic commuting graphs are isoclinic. However, Eamonn O’Brien (personal communication) has shown that even this is false. The groups SmallGroup(64,18) and SmallGroup(64,215) have nilpotency class 22 and isomorphic commuting graphs, but are not isoclinic (their derived quotients have exponent 44 and 22 respectively). He also has counterexamples with orders 363^{6} and 565^{6}.

Question 4

What can be said about pairs of groups with isomorphic commuting graphs? Do non-isoclinic examples exist for all orders p6p^{6} with pp prime?

Part II Forbidden subgraphs

10 Preliminaries

A number of important graph classes can be defined either structurally or in terms of forbidden induced subgraphs. Here are structural descriptions.

  1. (a)

    Γ\Gamma is called a cograph if it can be built from 11-vertex graphs by the operations of disjoint union and complementation.

  2. (b)

    Γ\Gamma is called a chordal graph provided that Γ\Gamma contains no induced cycles of length greater than 33; in other words, any cycle of length at least 44 contains a chord.

The characterization by forbidden subgraphs is a composite of results from [37, 28, 75, 27].

Proposition 10.1
  1. (a)

    A graph is a cograph if and only if it forbids P4P_{4}.

  2. (b)

    A graph is chordal if and only if it forbids {Cn:n≥4}\{C_{n}:n\geq 4\}.

Since a cycle of length 55 or more contains a 44-vertex path, we have the following observation.

Observation 3

If a graph is {P4,C4}\{P_{4},C_{4}\}-free, then it is chordal.

We conclude this section with a general remark. In the commuting graph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) of a group GG, elements of the centre Z⁡(G)Z(G) are dominating vertices; this is the reason why, to investigate questions about connectedness, they are excluded. However, in our case, it doesn’t matter:

Proposition 10.2
  1. (a)

    The class of groups whose commuting graph is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free is subgroup-closed.

  2. (b)

    If no graph in ℱ\mathcal{F} has a dominating vertex, then the class of groups with ℱ\mathcal{F}-free commuting graph is independent of whether vertices in Z⁡(G)Z(G) are included or excluded.

Proof 24

(a) This is immediate from the fact that, if HH is a subgroup of GG, then Γ⁡(H)\Gamma(H) is an induced subgraph of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). (We remark that the same result holds for various other graphs such as the power graph, enhanced power graph, nilpotency and solvability graphs. But it does not hold for yet others such as the generating graph or the deep commuting graph.)

(b) If XX is an induced subgraph of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G), then vertices of X∩Z⁡(G)X\cap Z(G) would be dominating vertices in XX. ∎

In the cases we are interested in (chordal graphs and cographs), the excluded subgraphs are paths and cycles with more than three vertices. None of these have dominating vertices, so we can take the vertex set of the commuting graph to be all of GG, but to decide if it has any of these properties we can delete vertices in Z⁡(G)Z(G).

Also to prove main results of this paper, we need the following assertion which generalizes a result obtained by Wielandt [82] in 1939.

Proposition 10.3

Let GG be a finite group. Assume that one of the following statements holds:

  1. (a)

    Z⁡(G)=1Z(G)=1;

  2. (b)

    G=G′G=G^{\prime}.

Then CAut(G)​(Inn(G))=1C_{\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G)}(\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G))=1.

Proof 25

Let ϕ\phi be an automorphism of GG which commutes with each inner automorphism of GG. Then for each g,h∈Gg,h\in G, we have

ϕ​(h)g=ϕ⁡(hg)=ϕ​(h)ϕ⁡(g),\phi(h)^{g}=\phi(h^{g})=\phi(h)^{\phi(g)},

i. e. [g,ϕ]=g−1​ϕ​(g)∈Z⁡(G)[g,\phi]=g^{-1}\phi(g)\in Z(G) and ϕ⁡(g)=g⋅zg\phi(g)=g\cdot z_{g} for some zg∈Z⁡(G)z_{g}\in Z(G) (depending of gg).

If Z⁡(G)=1Z(G)=1, then zg=1z_{g}=1 for each gg, therefore ϕ\phi is trivial and CAut(G)​(Inn(G))=1C_{\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G)}(\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G))=1, as required.

Now assume that GG is perfect, i.e. G′=GG^{\prime}=G. Note that ϕ⁡([x,y])=[ϕ⁡(x),ϕ⁡(y)]=[x,y]\phi([x,y])=[\phi(x),\phi(y)]=[x,y] for each x,y∈Gx,y\in G. Since GG is generated by commutators, we have zg=1z_{g}=1 for each gg. Thus, again ϕ\phi is trivial and so, CAut(G)​(Inn(G))=1C_{\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(G)}(\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(G))=1. ∎

11 Structure of groups whose commuting graphs are cographs or chordal graphs

In this section, we will investigate the group-theoretical structure of a group whose commuting graph is a cograph or a chordal graph. In particular, in some sense, the class of such groups generalizes the class of finite solvable groups.

First, we investigate special cases of groups like direct and central products and Frobenius groups whose commuting graph is a cograph or a chordal graph, and then prove the general structure theorem.

11.1 Direct and central products

Observation 4

Let AA be an abelian group. Then Γ⁡(A×G)\Gamma(A\times G) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph) if and only if Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph).

Lemma 11.1

Let HH and KK be non-abelian groups. Then Γ⁡(H×K)\Gamma(H\times K) has an induced subgraph isomorphic to P4P_{4} and an induced subgraph isomorphic to C4C_{4}.

Proof 26

Let aa and bb be non-commuting elements of GG, and uu and vv non-commuting elements of HH. Then

(a,u)∼(eH,u)∼(b,eK)∼(eH,v)(a,u)\sim(e_{H},u)\sim(b,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},v)

is an induced path with four vertices, and

(a,eK)∼(eH,u)∼(b,eK)∼(eH,v)∼(a,eK)(a,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},u)\sim(b,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},v)\sim(a,e_{K})

is an induced cycle of length 44, as desired. ∎

By Lemma 11.1 and Observation 4, the following result holds.

Proposition 11.2

Let HH and KK be groups. Then

  1. (a)

    Γ⁡(H×K)\Gamma(H\times K) is a cograph if and only if one of HH and KK is abelian and the commuting graph of the other is P4P_{4}-free;

  2. (b)

    Γ⁡(H×K)\Gamma(H\times K) is chordal if and only if one of HH and KK is abelian and the other is CnC_{n}-free for all n≥4n\geq 4.

Recall that a finite nilpotent group is the direct product of its Sylow subgroups. Thus, Proposition 11.2 implies the following result.

Corollary 11.3

Let GG be a non-abelian nilpotent group. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph) if and only if there exists exactly one non-abelian Sylow subgroup in GG whose commuting graph is P4P_{4}-free (resp. CnC_{n}-free for all n≥4n\geq 4), while the other Sylow subgroups are abelian.

We saw in the first part the definition of the strong product of graphs and the fact that the commuting graph of G×HG\times H is Γ⁡(G)⊠Γ⁡(H)\Gamma(G)\boxtimes\Gamma(H) (Proposition 5.1).

We can extend this to central products as follows. Let 𝔑2\mathfrak{N}_{2} be the class of all finite nilpotent groups of nilpotency class at most 22 (thus, the class consists of finite abelian groups and finite non-abelian groups of nilpotency class 22).

Lemma 11.4

Let HH and KK be two groups not in the class 𝔑2\mathfrak{N}_{2}. Then Γ⁡(H∘K)\Gamma(H\circ K) is neither a cograph nor a chordal graph.

Proof 27

By assumption, we can choose a,b∈Ha,b\in H such that the commutator [a,b][a,b] is not in the centre of HH, and similarly u,v∈Ku,v\in K. Then

(a,u)∼(a,eK)∼(eH,v)∼(b,v)(a,u)\sim(a,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},v)\sim(b,v)

carries a subgroup P4P_{4} of Γ⁡(H×K)\Gamma(H\times K) such that the projection to H∘KH\circ K is an isomorphism, and also

(a,eK)∼(eH,u)∼(b,eK)∼(eH,v)∼(a,eK)(a,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},u)\sim(b,e_{K})\sim(e_{H},v)\sim(a,e_{K})

is a subgraph isomorphic to C4C_{4} which projects isomorphically to H∘KH\circ K. ∎

11.2 Frobenius groups

In this subsection we investigate when the commuting graph of a Frobenius group is a cograph or a chordal graph. We use the structure of the commuting graphs of Frobenius groups established in Theorem 6.2. We prove the following assertion.

Proposition 11.5

Let GG be a Frobenius group with Frobenius complement HH and Frobenius kernel KK and ℱ\mathcal{F} be a collection of graphs such that no graph in ℱ\mathcal{F} has a dominating vertex. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free if and only if Γ⁡(K)\Gamma(K) is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free and Γ⁡(H)\Gamma(H) is ℱ\mathcal{F}-free.

Proof 28

This is clear from our remarks about dominating vertices and the fact (observed in Theorem 6.2) that Γ⁡(G∖{1})\Gamma(G\setminus\{1\}) is the disjoint union of Γ⁡(H∖{1})\Gamma(H\setminus\{1\}) and |H||H| copies of Γ⁡(K∖{1})\Gamma(K\setminus\{1\}).

Corollary 11.6

Let GG be a Frobenius group with Frobenius complement HH and Frobenius kernel KK. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph (resp. chordal graph) if and only if Γ⁡(K)\Gamma(K) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph) and Γ⁡(H)\Gamma(H) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph).

Remark 8

Since KK is nilpotent, Corollary 11.3 gives a criterion for Γ⁡(K)\Gamma(K) to be a cograph (resp. a chordal graph).

Question 5

For which Frobenius groups is the commuting graph a cograph or a chordal graph?

11.3 A general structure theorem

The main result of this section is the following theorem.

Theorem 11.7

Let GG be a finite group such that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph), and let F⁡(G)F(G) be the Fitting subgroup of GG.

  1. (a)

    One of the following statements holds:

    1. (i)

      CG​(F⁡(G))=Z⁡(F⁡(G))C_{G}(F(G))=Z(F(G));

    2. (ii)

      F⁡(G)F(G) is of nilpotent class at most 22 and G/F⁡(G)G/F(G) is almost simple; in particular, GG has a unique non-abelian composition factor.

  2. (b)

    If Soc(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Soc}}(G) is non-abelian, then GG has a normal subgroup N=A×SN=A\times S, where AA is abelian, SS is simple and Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph), such that G/NG/N is isomorphic to a subgroup of Out(S)\mathop{\mathrm{Out}}(S) and, therefore, G/NG/N is solvable.

Proof 29

Let F∗​(G)F^{*}(G) be the generalized Fitting subgroup of GG. Let H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} be distinct elements from Comp(G)\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G). By [3, 31.5], H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} commute, therefore ⟨H1,H2⟩=H1∘H2\langle H_{1},H_{2}\rangle=H_{1}\circ H_{2} is a subgroup of GG. By Lemma 11.4, Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is neither a cograph nor a chordal graph, a contradiction to Proposition 10.2. Thus, |Comp(G)|≤1|\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G)|\leq 1.

If |Comp(G)|=0|\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G)|=0, then F∗​(G)=F​(G)F^{*}(G)=F(G), and because we have CG​(F∗​(G))≤F∗​(G)C_{G}(F^{*}(G))\leq F^{*}(G) by [3, 31.13], statement (a)(i) holds.

Assume that |Comp(G)|=1|\mathop{\mathrm{Comp}}(G)|=1. Then GG has a quasisimple characteristic subgroup N=E⁡(G)N=E(G). Consider C=CG​(N)C=C_{G}(N), which is a normal subgroup of GG. Let H=⟨N,C⟩=N∘CH=\langle N,C\rangle=N\circ C. By Proposition 10.2 and Lemma 11.4, CC is nilpotent of nilpotency class at most 22, therefore C≤F⁡(G)C\leq F(G). On the other hand, F⁡(G)≤CF(G)\leq C by (1). Thus, C=F⁡(G)C=F(G) and, therefore G/F⁡(G)G/F(G) is a subgroup of Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) which has a simple normal subgroup H/C≅N/Z⁡(N)H/C\cong N/Z(N).

Now we show that Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) is an almost simple group and Soc(Aut(N))≅N/Z⁡(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Soc}}(\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N))\cong N/Z(N). Indeed, N/Z⁡(N)≅Inn(N)N/Z(N)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N) is a normal subgroup of Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) and N/Z⁡(N)N/Z(N) is simple. By Proposition 10.3, we have

Aut(N)≅Aut(N)/CAut(N)​(Inn(N))\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N)/C_{\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N)}(\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N))

is a subgroup of Aut(Inn(N))≅Aut(N/Z⁡(N))\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N))\cong\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N/Z(N)). So, we have that Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) is a subgroup of an almost simple subgroup Aut(N/Z⁡(N))\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N/Z(N)) which contains a normal subgroup Inn(N)≅N/Z⁡(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N)\cong N/Z(N). Thus, Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) is an almost simple group with socle N/Z⁡(N)N/Z(N), as required.

So, G/F⁡(G)G/F(G) is isomorphic to a subgroup of Aut(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(N) which is almost simple with socle isomorphic to Inn(N)\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N) and contains a subgroup H/F⁡(G)≅Inn(N)H/F(G)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{Inn}}(N), therefore G/F⁡(G)G/F(G) is almost simple. Thus, statement (a)(ii) holds.

Now we prove statement (b). Assume that L=Soc(G)L=\mathop{\mathrm{Soc}}(G) is non-abelian. Then L=A×SL=A\times S, where AA is abelian and SS is the direct product of non-abelian simple groups, moreover, both AA and SS are normal subgroups of GG. By Propositions 10.2 and 11.2, SS is simple and Γ⁡(S)\Gamma(S) is a cograph (resp. a chordal graph). If C=CG​(S)C=C_{G}(S), then C⊴GC\unlhd G and C∩S=1C\cap S=1 since SS is simple. Thus, N=S​C=S×CN=SC=S\times C is a normal subgroup of GG. By Proposition 10.2, Γ⁡(N)\Gamma(N) is also a cograph (resp. a chordal graph). Using Proposition 11.2, we conclude that CC is abelian. Moreover, G/CG/C is isomorphic to a subgroup of Aut(S)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}(S) which is almost simple, therefore G/NG/N is isomorphic to a subgroup of Out(S)\mathop{\mathrm{Out}}(S). Thus, by the Schreier Conjecture (Theorem 2.1), G/NG/N is solvable, and therefore statement (b) holds. ∎

Remark 9

If Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph, then in statement (b)(b) of Theorem 11.7 the group G/NG/N is cyclic. This result follows from the classification of finite simple groups whose commuting graphs are cographs, see Theorem 12.16 below.

The following problem is of interest.

Problem 1

Classify finite simple groups whose commuting graphs are chordal.

12 Simple groups whose commuting graph is a cograph or a chordal graph

In this section, we investigate when the commuting graph of a simple sporadic or alternating group is a cograph or a chordal graph, and then obtain a complete classification of finite simple groups whose commuting graph is a cograph.

12.1 CA-groups and AC-groups

A group GG is a CA-group if the centralizer of every non-identity element of GG is abelian. Another name is CT-groups, since they are the groups for which the commutation relation on non-identity elements is transitive. (If x∼y∼zx\sim y\sim z in the CA-group GG, then x,z∈CG​(y)x,z\in C_{G}(y), so xx and zz commute. The converse is similar.)

If GG is a CA-group, then the induced subgraph Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) on non-identity elements is a disjoint union of complete graphs. As a result, we see:

Proposition 12.1

Let GG be a CA-group. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph, chordal, and perfect.

CA-groups played an important historical role in developing techniques for attacking problems on finite groups; they are now well-understood. From results of Weisner [81], Brauer, Suzuki and Wall [13] and Suzuki [76], we obtain:

Proposition 12.2

A finite CA-group GG satisfies one of the following:

  1. (a)

    GG is abelian;

  2. (b)

    GG is a Frobenius group with abelian Frobenius kernel and cyclic Frobenius complement; or

  3. (c)

    G≅PSL2(q)G\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) for qq a power of 22.

More generally, GG is said to be an AC-group if CG​(x)C_{G}(x) is abelian for every element x∈G∖Z⁡(G)x\in G\setminus Z(G). This is a weaker condition, though clearly a group with trivial centre is an AC-group if and only if it is a CA-group.

AC-groups were investigated by Schmidt [67] and Rocke [66]. (Schmidt investigated groups in which two maximal centralizers intersect just in Z⁡(G)Z(G); it is not hard to see that, for finite groups, this is equivalent to the AC property.) Abdollahi et al. [2] investigated the connection of this property with the non-commuting graph, the complement of the commuting graph. The classification of the AC-groups is not as complete as that of CA-groups, but the cited authors have proved a number of results about these groups.

From our point of view, AC-groups are as good as CA-groups:

Proposition 12.3

Let GG be an AC-group. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph and a chordal graph.

Proof 30

By Proposition 10.2, it suffices to consider the induced subgraph on the set G∖Z⁡(G)G\setminus Z(G); and this graph is a disjoint union of complete graphs. ∎

Here is a simple general result which we will use.

Proposition 12.4

Let GG be a finite group with the property that every non-identity element of G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G) has cyclic centralizer. Then GG is an AC-group.

Proof 31

Take a∈G∖Z⁡(G)a\in G\setminus Z(G). Then Z​(G)≤CG​(a)Z(G)\leq C_{G}(a), and CG​(a)/Z⁡(G)≤CG​(a​Z​(G))C_{G}(a)/Z(G)\leq C_{G}(aZ(G)) (in G/Z⁡(G)G/Z(G)); so CG​(a)/Z​(G)C_{G}(a)/Z(G) is cyclic, whence CG​(a)C_{G}(a) is abelian. ∎

12.2 Generalized dihedral groups and generalized quaternion groups

In this subsection we show that these groups are AC-groups, so that their commuting graphs are cographs as well as chordal graphs.

Proposition 12.5

Let D⁡(A)D(A) be the generalized dihedral group as presented in Equation (4). Then D⁡(A)D(A) is an AC-group. Hence Γ⁡(D⁡(A))\Gamma(D(A)) is a cograph as well as a chordal graph. In particular, the commuting graph of a dihedral group is a cograph as well as a chordal graph.

Proof 32

The centre of D⁡(A)D(A) is the subgroup TT of AA consisting of elements of orders 11 or 22. If we remove it, then A∖TA\setminus T is a clique, and the elements outside AA fall into cliques of the form ⟨t,T⟩∖T\langle t,T\rangle\setminus T for t∉At\notin A; there are no edges between these cliques. So the induced subgraph is a disjoint union of complete graphs. Now Proposition 10.2 gives the result.∎

Proposition 12.6

Let Q4​mQ_{4m} be the generalized quaternion group as presented in Equation (5). Then Q4​mQ_{4m} is an AC-group. Hence Γ⁡(Q4​m)\Gamma(Q_{4m}) is a cograph as well as a chordal graph.

Proof 33

The proof is similar to the preceding theorem. We find that, with G=Q4​mG=Q_{4m}, we have Z⁡(G)={e,xm}Z(G)=\{e,x^{m}\} (Observation 2); for 1≤i≤2​m−11\leq i\leq 2m-1 and i≠mi\neq m, we find that CG​(xi)=⟨x⟩C_{G}(x^{i})=\langle x\rangle, while for 0≤i≤2​m−10\leq i\leq 2m-1 we have CG​(xi​y)=⟨xi​y⟩={e,xi​y,xm,xm+i​y}C_{G}(x^{i}y)=\langle x^{i}y\rangle=\{e,x^{i}y,x^{m},x^{m+i}y\}. So again the induced subgraph on G∖Z⁡(G)G\setminus Z(G) consists of a complete graph of size 2​m−22m-2 together with mm disjoint edges. ∎

12.3 Symmetric groups and alternating groups

Proposition 12.7

Γ⁡(Sn)\Gamma(S_{n}) is a cograph if and only if n≤3n\leq 3.

Proof 34

Proposition 10.2 shows that it is enough to show that Γ⁡(S3)\Gamma(S_{3}) is a cograph but Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}) is not (since Sn−1≤SnS_{n-1}\leq S_{n} for any nn). By Proposition 12.5, we have that Γ⁡(S3)\Gamma(S_{3}) is a cograph as S3≅D6S_{3}\cong D_{6}. As Sn−1≤SnS_{n-1}\leq S_{n}, Proposition 10.2 shows that if n≤3n\leq 3, then Γ⁡(Sn)\Gamma(S_{n}) is a cograph. In Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}),

(12)∼(12)​(34)∼(13)​(24)∼(13)(12)\sim(12)(34)\sim(13)(24)\sim(13)

is an induced path isomorphic to P4P_{4}.∎

Proposition 12.8

Γ⁡(Sn)\Gamma(S_{n}) is a chordal graph if and only if n≤4n\leq 4.

Proof 35

It is easy to see that

(12)∼(34)∼(15)∼(24)∼(35)∼(12)(12)\sim(34)\sim(15)\sim(24)\sim(35)\sim(12)

is an induced cycle isomorphic to C5C_{5} in Γ⁡(S5)\Gamma(S_{5}). As in Proposition 12.7, it suffices to prove that Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}) is a chordal graph. Note that in Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}), for any non-central element, the cycle type of this element must be one of

{(i​j),(i​j)​(k​l),(i​j​k),(i​j​k​l)},\{(ij),(ij)(kl),(ijk),(ijkl)\}, (10)

where {i,j,k,l}={1,2,3,4}\{i,j,k,l\}=\{1,2,3,4\}. Moreover, it is easy to see that

CS4​((i​j))={e,(i​j),(k​l),(i​j)​(k​l)},CS4​((i​j))={e,(i​j),(k​l),(i​j)​(k​l)}C_{S_{4}}((ij))=\{e,(ij),(kl),(ij)(kl)\},C_{S_{4}}((ij))=\{e,(ij),(kl),(ij)(kl)\}
CS4​((i​j​k​l))=⟨(i​j​k​l)⟩C_{S_{4}}((ijkl))=\langle(ijkl)\rangle (11)

and

CS4​((i​j)​(k​l))={e,(i​j),(k​l),(i​j)​(k​l),(i​k)​(j​l),(i​l)​(j​k),(i​k​j​l),(i​l​j​k)}.C_{S_{4}}((ij)(kl))=\{e,(ij),(kl),(ij)(kl),(ik)(jl),(il)(jk),(ikjl),(iljk)\}.

Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}) contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to CnC_{n} with n≥4n\geq 4, say Δ\Delta. Let a,b,c,da,b,c,d be 44 distinct vertices of Δ\Delta. Then CS4​(x)C_{S_{4}}(x) is non-abelian for any x∈{a,b,c,d}x\in\{a,b,c,d\}. Note that every centralizer in (11) is abelian. It follows from (10) that every element in {a,b,c,d}\{a,b,c,d\} has cycle type (i​j)​(k​l)(ij)(kl), which is impossible because S4S_{4} has precisely three elements that are the product of two disjoint cycles. ∎

Proposition 12.9

The following are equivalent:

(a)(a) Γ⁡(An)\Gamma(A_{n}) is a cograph;

(b)(b) Γ⁡(An)\Gamma(A_{n}) is a chordal graph;

(c)(c) n≤5n\leq 5.

Proof 36

The group A5A_{5} is a CA-group (it is easily checked from [29] that all its non-abelian subgroups have trivial centre), so the result for n=5n=5 follows from Proposition 12.2. Moreover, An≤A5A_{n}\leq A_{5} for n≤5n\leq 5, so the result follows for these groups as well.

On the other hand, in Γ⁡(A6)\Gamma(A_{6}), it is easy to verify that

(12)​(56)∼(12)​(34)∼(13)​(24)∼(13)​(56)(12)(56)\sim(12)(34)\sim(13)(24)\sim(13)(56)

is an induced path isomorphic to P4P_{4}. Also, it is not hard to verify that

(34)​(56)∼(12)​(56)∼(15)​(26)∼(26)​(34)∼(24)​(36)\displaystyle(34)(56)\sim(12)(56)\sim(15)(26)\sim(26)(34)\sim(24)(36)
∼(15)​(24)∼(12)​(45)∼(36)​(45)∼(34)​(56)\displaystyle\sim(15)(24)\sim(12)(45)\sim(36)(45)\sim(34)(56)

is an induced cycle isomorphic to C8C_{8}, so Γ⁡(A6)\Gamma(A_{6}) is not chordal. Now A6≤AnA_{6}\leq A_{n} for n>6n>6, so Γ⁡(An)\Gamma(A_{n}) is neither a cograph nor chordal for n≥6n\geq 6, by Proposition 10.2. ∎

In the commuting graph of A6A_{6} with the identity removed, the elements of orders 33 and 55 induce a disjoint union of cliques, while an element of order 44 is joined only to its inverse and square. So induced cycles on more than three vertices must consist of elements of order 22. We can describe the induced subgraph on these elements as follows.

Proposition 12.10

Let Δ\Delta be the induced subgraph of the commuting graph of A6A_{6} on the set of involutions. Then Δ\Delta is isomorphic to the line graph of Tutte’s 88-cage [80]. In particular, an induced cycle in Γ⁡(A6)\Gamma(A_{6}) with length greater than 33 has length at least 88.

Proof 37

Tutte’s 88-cage TT (the smallest cubic graph with girth 88) can be defined as follows. Vertices are odd involutions in the symmetric group S6S_{6}; these are of two types, transpositions and products of three transpositions. Two vertices are joined if one is a product of three transpositions, one of which is the other. Further information on this graph can be found in [16, p. 209].

There is a bijection between vertices of Δ\Delta and edges of TT: for example, the vertex (12)​(34)(12)(34) of Δ\Delta corresponds to the edge {(12)​(34)​(56),(56)}\{(12)(34)(56),(56)\} of TT. A simple check shows that this bijection is an isomorphism between Δ\Delta and the line graph of TT.

Now it is easily checked that TT has girth 88; it is in fact the incidence graph of the unique generalized quadrangle of order 22. It follows that, apart from triangles coming from three edges through a vertex of TT, the shortest cycles in Δ\Delta have length 88.

The fact that this holds for the graph Γ⁡(A6)\Gamma(A_{6}) now follows from the remarks before the Proposition.∎

Remark 10

However, Γ⁡(A7)\Gamma(A_{7}) has an induced cycle isomorphic to C6C_{6}, such as (123)∼(456)∼(127)∼(345)∼(126)∼(457)∼(123)(123)\sim(456)\sim(127)\sim(345)\sim(126)\sim(457)\sim(123). Also, Γ⁡(A8)\Gamma(A_{8}) has an induced cycle isomorphic to C4C_{4}, such as (12)​(34)∼(567)∼(348)∼(12)​(56)∼(12)​(34)(12)(34)\sim(567)\sim(348)\sim(12)(56)\sim(12)(34).

12.4 Sporadic groups

In this subsection, we resolve the question for the sporadic simple groups.

Proposition 12.11

If GG is a sporadic simple group, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is neither a cograph nor a chordal graph.

Proof 38

There are 2626 sporadic simple groups. Observe that S5S_{5} is a subgroup of the Mathieu group M11M_{11} by using information in the 𝔸​𝕋​𝕃​𝔸​𝕊\mathbb{ATLAS} of finite groups [29]. Also, note that the fact that the Mathieu group M11M_{11} is a subgroup of all the other sporadic simple groups except M22M_{22}, J1J_{1}, J2J_{2}, J3J_{3}, H​eHe, R​uRu and T​hTh. Thus, by Proposition 10.2 and Propositions 12.7 and 12.8, the commuting graph of a sporadic simple group containing M11M_{11} is neither a cograph nor a chordal graph.

Now by [29] again, it is easy to observe that A7≤M22A_{7}\leq M_{22}, D6×D10≤J1D_{6}\times D_{10}\leq J_{1}, A4×A5≤J2A_{4}\times A_{5}\leq J_{2}, A6≤J3A_{6}\leq J_{3}, S6≤H​eS_{6}\leq He, A8≤R​uA_{8}\leq Ru, S5≤T​hS_{5}\leq Th. Thus, it follows from Proposition 10.2, Lemma 11.1 and Proposition 12.9 that the commuting graphs of these 77 sporadic simple groups are neither cographs nor chordal graphs, as desired. ∎

12.5 Simple groups of Lie type whose commuting graph is a cograph

Now we turn to simple groups of Lie type. In this analysis, we only consider cographs, not chordal graphs.

Proposition 12.12

Let G=PSL2(q)G=\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q), with q≥4q\geq 4. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph if and only if either qq is a power of 22 or q=5q=5.

Note that PSL2(5)≅PSL2(4)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(5)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(4).

Proof 39

The subgroup structure of PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) was determined by Dickson [32], and can be found, for example, in [14].

Suppose first that q≥4q\geq 4 is a power of 22. Then every non-trivial element of PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) has order 22 or a divisor of q−1q-1 and q+1q+1. Also, the centralizers of involutions of PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) are elementary abelian groups with order qq, and the centralizers of other non-trivial elements of PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) are cyclic of order q−1q-1 or q+1q+1. It follows that in this case PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) is a CA-group, and so by Proposition 12.2, Γ⁡(PSL2(q))\Gamma(\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q)) is a cograph.

Suppose next that qq is odd at least 55. Let ϵ∈{+1,−1}\epsilon\in\{+1,-1\} be chosen so that q+ϵ​1q+\epsilon 1 is divisible by 44. Note that PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) contains a Klein group such that the centralizers of its involutions are dihedral groups D2​(q+ϵ​1)D_{2(q+\epsilon 1)} which contain disjoint cyclic groups of order (q+ϵ)/2(q+\epsilon)/2. If q>5q>5, then (q+ε)/2>2(q+\varepsilon)/2>2. So two involutions together with generators of cyclic groups of order (q+ϵ)/2(q+\epsilon)/2 in their centralizers induce a path of length 44. (The list of subgroups of GG shows that these generators do not commute.) So if q>5q>5 is odd, then Γ⁡(PSL2(q))\Gamma(\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q)) is not a cograph. ∎

Remark 11

It is well-known that PSL2(2)≅S3\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(2)\cong S_{3} and PSL2(3)≅A4\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(3)\cong A_{4}, therefore their commuting graphs are cographs by Propositions 12.7 and 12.9, respectively.

Proposition 12.13

Let GG be either PSL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(q) or a group of Lie type of BN-rank at least 33. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph.

Proof 40

We begin by showing that, if G=SL3(q)G=\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{3}(q), then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph.

Suppose first that q∉{2,4}q\notin\{2,4\}. Choose a non-zero element a∈GF(q)a\in\mathop{\mathrm{GF}}\nolimits(q) such that a3≠1a^{3}\neq 1, and let b=a−2b=a^{-2}, so that b≠ab\neq a.

Consider the four elements g1,…,g4g_{1},\ldots,g_{4} given by

(110010001),(a000a000b),(b000a000a),(100011001).\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&1&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}a&0&0\\ 0&a&0\\ 0&0&b\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}b&0&0\\ 0&a&0\\ 0&0&a\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&0&0\\ 0&1&1\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right).

It is clear that all of them belong to GG, and that g1∼g2∼g3∼g4g_{1}\sim g_{2}\sim g_{3}\sim g_{4} in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G). A short calculation gives the commutators of the other three pairs; none of them is trivial. So we have an induced path in Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G).

But the argument gives more. In fact none of the commutators is a scalar matrix, so if ZZ is any subgroup of the centre of GG (the group of scalar matrices), then we also have an induced path in Γ⁡(G/Z)\Gamma(G/Z), so that Γ⁡(G/Z)\Gamma(G/Z) is not a cograph. In particular, Γ⁡(PSL3(q))\Gamma(\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(q)) is not a cograph.

Now we can cover the remaining two cases. Since PSL3(2)≅PSL2(7)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(2)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(7), the commuting graph of PSL3(2)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(2) is not a cograph. Also, PSL3(2)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(2) is a subgroup of both SL3(4)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{3}(4) and PSL3(4)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(4), so their commuting graphs are not cographs either.

For the remainder of the proof, we use the Levi decomposition of parabolic subgroups of groups with BN-pairs (see [26, Section 8.5]). The Borel subgroup HH of such a group is generated by the root subgroups corresponding to the positive roots with respect to a fundamental system Π\Pi of roots. Parabolic subgroups PΦP_{\Phi} are those which contain HH; they are generated by HH together with the root subgroups corresponding to the negatives of a subset Φ\Phi of the negatives of the fundamental group. According to the Levi decomposition, PΦP_{\Phi} is the semidirect product of its unipotent radical by the Levi factor LΦL_{\Phi}, a group with BN-pair corresponding to the roots Φ\Phi. In the covering group, LΦL_{\Phi} may have a centre, which may or may not be killed when we factor out the centre of GG. (For example, SLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) has a parabolic subgroup corresponding to the first two roots, generated by all upper unitriangular matrices together with the lower unitriangular matrices with non-zero off-diagonal elements in positions 1,2,31,2,3 only. These generate SL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{3}(q); its image in PSLn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{n}(q) is either SL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{3}(q) or PSL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(q) depending on the congruence of nn and qq mod 33.)

Now the Coxeter–Dynkin diagram of any simple group GG of Lie type with BN-pair of rank at least 33 contains a single edge, corresponding to a root system of type A2A_{2}; so GG has a parabolic subgroup whose Levi factor is a central quotient of SL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{3}(q), as in the example above. From Proposition 10.2, we conclude that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph. ∎

Proposition 12.14

Let GG be a central quotient of SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q), with q>2q>2. Then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph.

Proof 41

Suppose that q>2q>2. We take the Hermitian form H⁡(x1,x2,x3)=x1q+1+x2q+1+x3q+1H(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=x_{1}^{q+1}+x_{2}^{q+1}+x_{3}^{q+1}. A diagonal matrix with diagonal entries (a,b,c)(a,b,c) preserves this form if and only if

aq+1=bq+1=cq+1=1,a^{q+1}=b^{q+1}=c^{q+1}=1,

and belongs to SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) if additionally a​b​c=1abc=1. So the set of such matrices forms a subgroup of SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) isomorphic to ℤq+12\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}^{2}, and its quotient in PSU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) is ℤq+1×ℤ(q+1)/gcd⁡(q+1,3)\mathbb{Z}_{q+1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{(q+1)/\gcd(q+1,3)}. We observe that (−1)q+1=1(-1)^{q+1}=1 (this is clear if qq is even and holds if qq is odd since then (−1)2=1(-1)^{2}=1).

Let a∈G​F​(q2)a\in GF(q^{2}) satisfy aq+1=1a^{q+1}=1, a3≠1a^{3}\neq 1, and let b=a−2b=a^{-2}, so that a≠ba\neq b. Now consider the four matrices g1g_{1}, …, g4g_{4} given by

(01010000−1),(a000a000b),(b000a000a),(−100001010).\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&-1\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}a&0&0\\ 0&a&0\\ 0&0&b\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}b&0&0\\ 0&a&0\\ 0&0&a\end{array}\right),\,\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-1&0&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{array}\right).

It is readily checked that all four matrices belong to SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q), and that g2g_{2} commutes with g1g_{1} and g3g_{3} while g3g_{3} commutes with g4g_{4}. The other pairs fail to commute; indeed in each case gi​gjg_{i}g_{j} is not a scalar multiple of gj​gig_{j}g_{i}. So the four matrices induce a P4P_{4} subgraph of the commuting graph, which remains as a P4P_{4} subgraph when the scalar matrices in SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) are factored out. ∎

Among the groups of Lie type, this leaves only those of ranks 11 or 22, and we have already handled PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q), PSL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(q), and PSU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) for q>2q>2. The remaining groups are:

  1. (a)

    PSp4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{4}(q);

  2. (b)

    PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) for n∈{4,5}n\in\{4,5\};

  3. (c)

    G2​(q)G_{2}(q), Sz(q)=B22​(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)={}^{2}B_{2}(q), R1​(q)=G22​(q)R_{1}(q)={}^{2}G_{2}(q), R2​(q)=F42​(q)R_{2}(q)={}^{2}F_{4}(q), and D43​(q){}^{3}D_{4}(q).

We have omitted the orthogonal groups here. For these satisfy

  1. (a)

    P​Ω3⁡(q)≅PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits_{3}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q);

  2. (b)

    P​Ω4+⁡(q)≅PSL2(q)×PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{+}_{4}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q)\times\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) and P​Ω4−⁡(q)≅PSL2(q2)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{-}_{4}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q^{2});

  3. (c)

    P​Ω5⁡(q)≅PSp4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits_{5}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{4}(q);

  4. (d)

    P​Ω6+⁡(q)≅PSL4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{+}_{6}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{4}(q);

  5. (e)

    P​Ω6−⁡(q)≅PSU4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{P}\Omega}\nolimits^{-}_{6}(q)\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{4}(q)

(see the 𝔸​𝕋​𝕃​𝔸​𝕊\mathbb{ATLAS} of Finite Groups [29]). So (a), (b) and (d) are covered by our earlier results, and (c) and (e) will be treated as symplectic or unitary groups.

Also G2​(q)G_{2}(q) contains a subgroup PSL3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{3}(q), and D43​(q){}^{3}D_{4}(q) contains G2​(q)G_{2}(q) [30, 51, 52], so their commuting graphs are not cographs, by Proposition 10.2 and Proposition 12.13.

We now finish off the classical groups.

The group PSp4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{4}(q) contains the central product of two copies of SL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{2}(q). (To see this, note that the 44-dimensional vector space can be written as the orthogonal direct sum of two 22-dimensional non-degenerate subspaces; so Sp4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sp}}\nolimits_{4}(q) contains SL2(q)×SL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{2}(q)\times\mathop{\mathrm{SL}}\nolimits_{2}(q). If qq is odd, take the quotient by {±I}\{\pm I\} to obtain a central product.) So its commuting graph is not a cograph, by Lemma 11.4.

For unitary groups, the PSU3(2)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{3}(2) is not simple; so for q=2q=2 it remains to deal with PSU4(2)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{4}(2) and PSU5(2)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{5}(2). The first is isomorphic to PSp4(3)\mathop{\mathrm{PSp}}\nolimits_{4}(3) [29], which we have dealt with. The second contains PSL2(11)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(11), see [29]. For q>2q>2, by Proposition 12.14 central quotients of SU3(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{3}(q) have commuting graphs which are not cographs. For n=5n=5, PSUn(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{n}(q) contains such a central quotient, obtained as above by writing the 55-dimensional unitary space as the sum of non-degenerate subspaces of dimensions 22 and 33. For n=4n=4, the space is the sum of two non-degenerate 22-dimensional subspaces, so PSU4(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSU}}\nolimits_{4}(q) contains a central product of two copies of SU2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{SU}}\nolimits_{2}(q). So the commuting graphs of these groups are not cographs either.

This concludes dealing with the classical groups.

We show next that the commuting graphs of the Suzuki groups are cographs.

Proposition 12.15

For each qq, the commuting graph of Sz(q)=B22​(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)={}^{2}B_{2}(q) is a cograph.

Proof 42

It is well-known that B22​(2)≅5:4{}^{2}B_{2}(2)\cong 5:4 is a Frobenius groups with cyclic kernel and cyclic complement. Therefore, by Proposition 11.5, Γ⁡(B22​(2))\Gamma({}^{2}B_{2}(2)) is a cograph. Thus, we can assume that q>2q>2.

The information used in the next two paragraphs is taken from Suzuki’s original paper [77]; it can also be found in [83, Section 4.2].

It suffices to show that the graph obtained by removing the identity is a cograph. Now B22​(q){}^{2}B_{2}(q) has maximal cyclic subgroups of orders q−1q-1 and q±2​q+1q\pm\sqrt{2q}+1, and every element of odd order lies in one of these; so the non-identity elements of odd order carry a disjoint union of complete graphs, with no edges to the remaining elements. The remaining elements have order 22 or 44, and since B22​(q){}^{2}B_{2}(q) is a CIT-group (one in which the centralizer of any involution is a 22-group), the remaining vertices lie in a disjoint union of copies of the commuting graph on P∖{e}P\setminus\{e\}, where PP is a Sylow 22-subgroup. Now |P|=q2|P|=q^{2} and |Z⁡(P)|=q|Z(P)|=q; elements of Z⁡(P)Z(P) are joined to every element of PP so we may remove them. The remaining elements of PP have order 44. If gg is one of these, then |CP​(g)|=2​q|C_{P}(g)|=2q and CP​(g)C_{P}(g) consists of two cosets of Z⁡(P)Z(P), so it is abelian; thus the elements of order 44 fall into q−1q-1 sets of size qq, each set a complete graph with no edges between different sets. Thus the graph is indeed a cograph. ∎

Next, the small Ree group R1​(q)=G22​(q)R_{1}(q)={}^{2}G_{2}(q), with qq an odd power of 33, is not simple for q=3q=3; for larger qq, it contains PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) (the centralizer of an involution in G22​(q){}^{2}G_{2}(q) is ℤ2×PSL2(q)\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q) [52]).

The Tits group F42​(2)′{}^{2}F_{4}(2)^{\prime} contains a subgroup isomorphic to PSL2(25)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(25) (this can be found in the 𝔸​𝕋​𝕃​𝔸​𝕊\mathbb{ATLAS} [29]); so its commuting graph is not a cograph. The group F42​(2)′{}^{2}F_{4}(2)^{\prime} is a subgroup of the large Ree group R2​(2d)=F42​(2d)R_{2}(2^{d})={}^{2}F_{4}(2^{d}) for all odd dd [56].

To summarize our results, combined with the earlier results on alternating and sporadic groups, and noting that A5≅PSL2(4)A_{5}\cong\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(4):

Theorem 12.16

Let GG be a non-abelian finite simple group. Then the commuting graph of GG is a cograph if and only if GG is isomorphic to PSL2(q)\mathop{\mathrm{PSL}}\nolimits_{2}(q), with qq a power of 22 and q>2q>2, or to Sz(q)=B22​(q)\mathop{\mathrm{Sz}}\nolimits(q)={}^{2}B_{2}(q), with qq an odd power of 22 and q>2q>2.

13 Appendix

In this section, we consider small groups whose commuting graphs are cographs or chordal graphs.

Lemma 13.1

If |G/Z⁡(G)|=p​q​r|G/Z(G)|=pqr with primes p,q,rp,q,r (not necessary distinct), then GG is an AC-group.

Proof 43

Let a∈G∖Z⁡(G)a\in G\setminus Z(G). It suffices to prove that CG​(a)C_{G}(a) is abelian. Note that Z⁡(G)⊆Z⁡(CG​(a))⊆CG​(a)<GZ(G)\subseteq Z(C_{G}(a))\subseteq C_{G}(a)<G. Since |G/Z⁡(G)|=p​q​r|G/Z(G)|=pqr, we have that |CG​(a)/Z⁡(G)|<p​q​r|C_{G}(a)/Z(G)|<pqr and |CG​(a)/Z​(G)||C_{G}(a)/Z(G)| is a divisor of p​q​rpqr. By the argument of Proposition 12.4, it suffices to consider the case where CG​(a)/Z​(G)C_{G}(a)/Z(G) is non-cyclic and has order p​qpq.

Then Z⁡(G)​aZ(G)a has order pp or qq. Thus, CG​(a)/Z​(G)C_{G}(a)/Z(G) has an element, say Z⁡(G)​bZ(G)b, such that CG​(a)/Z⁡(G)=⟨Z⁡(G)​b,Z⁡(G)​a⟩C_{G}(a)/Z(G)=\langle Z(G)b,Z(G)a\rangle. Note that [b,a]=1[b,a]=1. Hence, CG​(a)=⟨b,a,Z⁡(G)⟩C_{G}(a)=\langle b,a,Z(G)\rangle is an abelian group, as desired. ∎

A similar but easier proof shows the following.

Corollary 13.2

If |G/Z⁡(G)|=p​q|G/Z(G)|=pq or pp where p,qp,q are primes, then GG is an AC-group. In particular, If |G|=p​q|G|=pq or p​q​rpqr with primes p,q,rp,q,r, then GG is either an abelian group or an AC-group.

Note that these primes p,q,rp,q,r in Lemma 13.1 and Corollary 13.2 are not necessarily distinct. Now combining Corollary 13.2, Lemma 13.1 and Proposition 12.3, we have the following result.

Lemma 13.3

Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph as well as a chordal graph if one of the following holds:

  1. (a)

    GG is abelian;

  2. (b)

    |G|=p​q​r|G|=pqr or p​qpq, where p,q,rp,q,r are primes (not necessarily distinct);

  3. (c)

    |G/Z⁡(G)|=p|G/Z(G)|=p, p​qpq or p​q​rpqr, where p,q,rp,q,r are primes (not necessary distinct).

Proposition 13.4

If GG is a group of minimal order such that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph, then |G|=24|G|=24. In particular, for |G|≤24|G|\leq 24, Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph if and only if G≇S4G\ncong S_{4}.

Proof 44

Proposition 12.7 implies that Γ⁡(S4)\Gamma(S_{4}) is not a cograph. Thus, it suffices to show that if |G|≤24|G|\leq 24, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph if and only if G≇S4G\ncong S_{4}. Now suppose that |G|≤24|G|\leq 24. It follows from Lemma 13.3 that if |G|∉{16,24}|G|\notin\{16,24\}, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph. If |G|=16|G|=16, since a 22-group has non-trivial centre, we have that |G/Z⁡(G)|=2k|G/Z(G)|=2^{k} with k≤3k\leq 3, and so Lemma 13.3(c) implies that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph. Finally, we suppose that |G|=24|G|=24. Note that the fact that if G≇S4G\ncong S_{4}, then GG has non-trivial centre (cf. Burnside [19]). So, by Lemma 13.3(c), we have that if G≇S4G\ncong S_{4}, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a cograph, as desired. ∎

In this paper, we identify a finite group by the unique identifier of this finite group in SmallGroups library in the GAP system [38]. To be specific, the mm-th group of order nn is identified as SmallGroup[n,m][n,m], where [n,m][n,m] is called the GAP ID of the group.

By Lemma 11.1, Γ⁡(S3×S3)\Gamma(S_{3}\times S_{3}) is not a cograph. One can use the GAP system [38] to classify all finite groups GG satisfying |G|≤36|G|\leq 36 and Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a cograph; these groups are presented in Table 1. In particular, by Lemma 11.1, Γ⁡(S3×S3)\Gamma(S_{3}\times S_{3}) is not a cograph.

For the groups of order 3232, there are precisely two extra-special 22-groups D8∘D8D_{8}\circ D_{8} and D8∘Q8D_{8}\circ Q_{8} as follows:

D8∘D8\displaystyle D_{8}\circ D_{8} =\displaystyle= ⟨x,y,z,w|x2=y2=z2=w2=[x,y]2=[z,w]2=1,\displaystyle\langle x,y,z,w|x^{2}=y^{2}=z^{2}=w^{2}=[x,y]^{2}=[z,w]^{2}=1, (13)
[x,z]=[z,y]=[y,w]=[w,x]=1⟩\displaystyle[x,z]=[z,y]=[y,w]=[w,x]=1\rangle

where [x,y]=[z,w][x,y]=[z,w] is an involution belonging to Z⁡(D8∘D8)Z(D_{8}\circ D_{8});

D8∘Q8\displaystyle D_{8}\circ Q_{8} =\displaystyle= ⟨x,y,z,w|x2=y2=z4=w4=[x,y]2=[z,w]2=1,\displaystyle\langle x,y,z,w|x^{2}=y^{2}=z^{4}=w^{4}=[x,y]^{2}=[z,w]^{2}=1, (15)
[x,z]=[z,y]=[y,w]=[w,x]=1⟩\displaystyle[x,z]=[z,y]=[y,w]=[w,x]=1\rangle

where z2=w2=[x,y]=[z,w]z^{2}=w^{2}=[x,y]=[z,w] is an involution belonging to Z⁡(D8∘Q8)Z(D_{8}\circ Q_{8}).

Proposition 13.5

If GG is a group of minimal order such that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not a chordal graph, then |G|=32|G|=32. In particular, if G≅D8∘D8G\cong D_{8}\circ D_{8} or D8∘Q8D_{8}\circ Q_{8}, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not chordal.

Proof 45

Suppose that G≅D8∘D8G\cong D_{8}\circ D_{8} or D8∘Q8D_{8}\circ Q_{8}. Then by (13) and (15), it is easy to see that the induced subgraph of Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) by the set {x,y,z,w}\{x,y,z,w\} is isomorphic to C4C_{4}, which implies that Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is not chordal.

Now, it suffices to show that if |G|<32|G|<32, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a chordal graph. Suppose that |G|≤31|G|\leq 31. Note that a pp-group has non-trivial centre where pp is a prime. From Lemma 13.3, it follows that if |G|≠24|G|\neq 24, then Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is a chordal graph. Now consider |G|=24|G|=24. If G≅S4G\cong S_{4}, then by Proposition 12.8, Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is chordal. If G≇S4G\ncong S_{4}, then by Lemma 13.3 and the proof of Proposition 13.4, Γ⁡(G)\Gamma(G) is chordal, as desired. ∎

We have taken these computations further and determined, using GAP with the package GRAPE [73], the groups of order up to 128128 whose commuting graphs are not cographs. The numbers of groups are given in Table 2.
